subsubtopic: CALL FOR REVIEW OF FIREARMS PROVISIONS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Yesterday the Solicitor General in this House rightly condemned Bill C-451, a private member's bill on gun control which has been introduced by his party colleague, the former solicitor general, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That this House direct the Solicitor General to adopt the motion on the Order Paper in the name of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland to initiate a detailed review of firearm control provisions in the Criminal Code by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that this committee could conduct hearings across Canada, at which time the public, particularly in rural areas, could give their views and suggestions for necessary changes to the present gun laws which are cumbersome, expensive to administer, and ineffective except to harrass law-abiding people, since currently the criminal code does not restrict the use of firearms by the criminal element.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN PROCESSING CLAIMS

speechtext:

subsubtopic: DISPOSAL OF ARGUS FLEET
speechtext:
Crown Assets Disposal Corporation informs me as follows:
1.	The corporation did spend funds to maintain the Argus fleet to applicable engineering standards, (a) The funds spent were for the maintenance of the aircraft, (b) The total amount spent was $349,298.87. (c) $260,110.75 was paid to the IMP Group, Halifax, for maintenance services and $89,188.12 to the Department of National Defence (DND) for materials including the tie downs.
2.	Starting in the summer of 1980, an 18-month search for potential buyers was undertaken by CADC and External Affairs to sell the fleet as operational aircraft. A sale could not be negotiated. DND re-categorized the aircraft to scrap metal status and CADC distributed the offer to purchase to 400 known scrap dealers. The following nine bids were received and opened publicly in Halifax on September 25, 1981.
Associated Electronics and Metal Salvage Ltd.

Chatham Salvage Ltd.	49,200.00

3.	The standard terms and conditions of sale were used in the offer to purchase. In addition, the overriding conditions of sale were that: the aircraft were to be smelted or broken down on site to the extent that parts would not be recognizable as Argus aircraft parts, and that the project had to be completed no later than March 31, 1982.
4.	The amount of $71,936 was received for the scrap metal from Bristol Metal Industries of Canada. This was not the highest amount bid for the following reasons:
The first bidder, Associated Electronics and Metal Salvage Ltd. withdrew its offer.
The contract with the second bidder, Cirsic Inc. was terminated by CADC for default, and for that reason, the performance deposit for $50,000 made at the time of the contract award was forfeited by Cirsic Inc.
By the time, CADC approached the third bidder, the ten day validity period to accept the offer to purchase had elapsed.
Order Paper Questions
The original bid of the third bidder, Bristol Metal Industries of Canada Ltd., was $126,936; but due to the suddent depression in the metal market that occurred during CADC contract negotiations with the second highest bidder, Cirsic Inc., Bristol's revised bid of $71,936 was assessed as fair market value. However, before the contract was awarded to Bristol Metal Industries of Canada Ltd. CADC tried to contact the fourth bidder, Pine Creek Ventures Ltd., but this company situated in the Yukon was untraceable.
The remaining components were sold by lot to the highest bidders for an over-all sale value of $318,810.81. It is expected that the future sale of spare parts may generate additional revenues.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be introducing a motion. 1 am not sure what Your Honour has in the way of the eight amendments before you. I have one motion that will read:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-97, an act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977 and to provide for payments to certain provinces, be amended by deleting Clause 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"6. Sections 18 and 19 of the said act shall lapse on April 1, 1984."
I apologize if there has been any confusion in the procedure that 1 have been following, but I am sure Your Honour knows that this bill was just reported out of committee at one o'clock today. That shows the way in which committee members have been working at it since Monday night. They have been attempting to subject this bill to the kind of scrutiny in committee work that it indeed merits.
There has been very little time in which to refer the bill back to the House from committee and to have reproduced, for the work of the chamber, the various amendments that we wish to place before the House. 1 know hon. members of the New Democratic Party also wish to bring amendments forward. I mentioned that the bill had been sent from here to committee following second reading only on Monday night of this week. That meant that we had very little time in committee to give the kind of scrutiny to this bill that is necessary as it embodies such tremendous fiscal measures. It includes the allocation of some $105 billion from the federal government to the provinces for equalization and established programs financing over the next five years.
May I say to Your Honour that in our committee work we tried our best to give it intensive scrutiny, although we could not give it the kind of thorough examination that an extended period in committee could have provided. A number of witnesses appeared before us. With varying degrees of intensity, they all condemned the government's proposal to cut back substantially on funding of post-secondary education and health care by removing, as the government proposed, the revenue guarantee component of the established programs financing.
Let me mention some of the organizations which appeared before us in committee during the few days that were available to us. AH of the organizations which came before committee in the last few days were unanimous in their opposition to the cutbacks proposed by the federal government. The organizations included The Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Hospital Association, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Union of Public
Employees, the Canadian Federation of Students, The Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Medical Association. Your Honour will see, from the list of witnesses I have mentioned, that all of these organizations have a very real and deep interest in the funding of post-secondary education and health care across this country. They came before us in order to make known, in the strongest possible terms, their opposition to the proposals of the government. They were unanimous in their point of view. None of them agreed with what the government was doing. They all strenuously objected. Only three witnesses who came before us in that period of time supported the cutbacks. They were the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
I can understand the motivation of the Minister of Finance. He told the committee that all he wanted to do was to save money, regardless of the threat those savings posed to the standards of post-secondary education and health care across this country. His only interest was savings. He pushed the whole question of reduced standards of health care and postsecondary education in this country to one side. 1 suppose 1 can understand his motivation; he wants to grasp every penny he can get his hands on. However, what I cannot understand, what I find to be deplorable, and what I consider, indeed, to be a betrayal of their obligations as ministers responsible for the programs involved, is the meekness with which the Secretary of State and the Minister of National Health and Welfare surrendered to the Minister of Finance.
We propose to defend the clause that they have abandoned. We are doing so by the introduction of the amendment that 1 read at the beginning of this debate. We propose to defend the measure, which the government has decided to take out of the established programs financing, by introducing this motion:
That Bill C-97 be amended by deleting Clause 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"6. Sections 18 and 19 of the said act shall lapse on April 1, 1984."
That is very simple, both in intent and in expression. The amendment provides that the revenue guarantee component of established programs financing entitlement will continue for two more years.
We would prefer to go further. We would not stop with that amendment as 1 have read it if we had the option to do so. We would prefer to go further and make the continuation of that clause conditional on signed commitments by each province to increase their spending on health care and on post-secondary education during each of the two years, by percentages equal to the growth in the EPF escalator, which means about 1 1.5 per cent.
We would make that conditional on the provinces if we had the power to do so. However, while the government could have written such a condition into the bill presently before us when it was being drafted, an amendment by the opposition to accomplish that purpose would not be out of order. So I am regretful that indeed we cannot take that further step and
April 1, 1982

make it conditional upon the provinces to meet this obligation. We are therefore settling for a second best alternative.
During the two-year period that 1 have mentioned, we advocate an up to date federal-provincial inquiry into the funding needs of health care and post-secondary education. We advocate that that take place with full scope for input from interested groups and the public at large. That inquiry's findings would provide the basis for the proper division of responsibility for funding those services between the federal and provincial levels of government. It could also take testimony on the better definition of program conditions and on standards of health care and on what might be the appropriate national goals in post-secondary education.
I raised this question with the Secretary of State so that during this two-year period what we could come up with, I would hope, would be indeed a better definition of program conditions and standards of health care and the appropriate national goals in post-secondary education. Both of these, we trust, would command the support of both levels of government and lay the groundwork for serious negotiations on those points. We think that, given such an effort, the result would be funding arrangements better than those agreed on in 1977, because they would reflect a broad national consensus.
We also believe that agreement could be reached on national goals in post-secondary education and on standards of care and a more precise definition of conditions in the field of health. At the very least, we think that the attempt should be made. I would hope that it would be successful; nevertheless, if it should prove unsuccessful we would have two years in which the programs are funded by the federal government according to the commitment that it made in 1977-and that in itself would be an achievement. After March 31, 1984, the formula now embodied in this bill could be reintroduced if a better one is not renegotiated.
Should this amendment pass, sir, I believe each province has the moral obligation to fund both these programs at rates of growth at least equal to that of the EPF escalator. I know that a number of the provinces, even in the face of the termination of the revenue guarantee component of the established programs financing, have announced funding levels for 1982-83 which indeed meet that standard which I would make conditional on the provinces in the next two years. Assuming, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces respond to that moral obligation, 1 believe this amendment is a fair one. I do not believe the concessions asked are unreasonable in view of the importance of the programs at stake.
Many of us have had the opportunity to speak on this bill and to stress the importance that we lay on programs of postsecondary education and health care in Canada. They are important to every individual, to every Canadian citizen. Therefore, we are trying to ensure that the standards in both of these programs remain at the level they are at now or are improved upon. What we do not want to see-and this will happen if the measures that the government proposes come into effect-is the standards reduced.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
1 would be most remiss if I did not acknowledge that the amendment 1 am proposing was inspired by the Canadian Association of University Teachers, whose approach to this issue throughout has been a thoughtful and a constructive one.
During the committee hearings on this bill, Mr. Speaker, a number of comments were made by members and ministers opposite which I think are relevant to this amendment. Yesterday afternoon and this morning we heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare admit that the provinces would never have agreed to go from cost-sharing to block funding for hospital insurance in 1977, as the federal government wanted them to, without the commitment of the federal government to add partial compensation for the 1972 revenue guarantee to the EPF formula. They would never have agreed to take that step if they had not been guaranteed that there would be partial compensation for the 1972 revenue guarantee. That was to be built into the 1977 formula, as indeed it was, and the provinces expected it to continue.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare then argued that terminating that component of the formula-a step which will save the federal government $5.7 billion over the next five years-is not a breach of faith with the provinces. Although she admitted that it had been put in there in the first place as a part of a bargain with the provinces, she then went on to say that removing it is not a breach of faith with the provinces. She cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. In that argument we see once again the quality of this government's word. For on June 14, 1976, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) proposed the EPF formula, he argued that one of his reasons for doing so was that "the arrangements for these major programs should be placed on a more permanent footing". I repeat, he said "on a more permanent footing". Those were his words. So much, Mr. Speaker, for permanence and, indeed, so much for the word of the Prime Minister.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare went on to contend that the shortfall of $5.7 billion could somehow be absorbed without any impact on our health services in the provinces across the country. She argued that $5.7 billion less on health care and post-secondary education could somehow be handled without the standards being lowered in these two major programs. I am afraid, sir, that her faith in miracles is touching. 1 only wish it were matched by an appreciation of how much this bill is placing health care standards in jeopardy-because that, indeed, is what it is doing.
We also heard the Secretary of State say in committee that he could give no commitment as to what level of percentage increase in funding, if any, he will provide for post-secondary education after 1982-83. I pressed him on that, asking if the commitment beyond 1982-83 would be equal to, or an increase in, the EPF escalator. He refused to answer. He of course keeps in reserve the threat in the finance minister's budget paper on fiscal arrangements that the post-secondary education cash transfer will be frozen at its 1982-83 level after April 1, 1983, if negotiations with the provinces prove to be unsuccessful. This, after that cash transfer has already been reduced in 1982-83 by $180 million from its 1981-82 level.

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Therefore, we have a decrease this year in the actual cash payments that will be provided by the federal government for post-secondary education and we have no guarantee that after 1982-83 the transfers will not be frozen at a lower level than they were last year. That is the tremendous dilemma that faces all post-secondary institutions across the country, all students involved in those institutions, the faculty, the people who work in those organizations. That is the threat they now face.
First, they are being cut back this year in the level of funding. Second, the threat lies there that in future the level of funding may be held to what it is this year, which is reduced from what it was last year. At the same time, the Secretary of State expressed concern about interfering with the provinces' spending decisions on post-secondary education when 1 outlined this amendment to him. I told him what it was we wanted to accomplish with this amendment, to allow him two years to try and negotiate a better arrangement for postsecondary education financing and health care financing, to maintain the levels of spending at what they were last year and maintain the formula that was agreed to in 1977. However, he would not listen to that. He rebutted me with something to the effect that "I will cut my spending and then freeze it while you increase yours, but it is interference with provincial rights to say we will maintain our spending if you maintain yours while we negotiate". That was the intent of the comments by the Secretary of State yesterday.
I fail to understand his reason or his logic because it is not reasonable and it is not logical. Apparently the Secretary of State believes in a federalism of convenience. Perhaps 1 should not be too harsh on these ministers. After all, it is hard to be loyal when your government is implementing a policy which threatens to lead to the underfunding of programs you believe in. There is a real temptation to resort to the kind of sophistry we heard from these ministers in committee. If they truly believed in the programs they are supposed to defend, there was another path open to them. Instead of meekly following what the Minister of Finance told them they have to do, cut back on these major programs, a path was open to them, a path which people of more principle have taken in the past, and that is, after having lost the fight in cabinet, to resign in protest. If they truly believed in their programs, that is what they would have done.
Let me return to the comments of some of the backbench Liberal members of parliament who attended the committee hearings on this bill. They were very concerned, they said, that under the EPF arrangements the provinces had reduced their share of funding for post-secondary education. They did not see the use, they said, of extending the EPF arrangements because there was no guarantee that the money transferred to the provinces would be spent on the services for which it was intended. We heard that said over and over again. If that is the cause of their concern, I can understand it. If those are the reasons why they want changes to the EPF, I do not see how in conscience they can do other than vote for this amendment. It puts real moral pressure on the provinces to at least maintain, if not increase, their share of post-secondary education funding
during the next two years. The bill, as it stands, does not. The members who expressed concern as to whether the provinces might cut back on their funding, in this period of two years when moral pressure was brought to bear on the provinces to keep the spending at the level of the EPF escalator or to increase it beyond that, could see that being accomplished if they would support this amendment and give the negotiations a chance to take place in the next two years.
The amendment ensures that federal EPF funding will continue to rise according to the formula agreed to in 1977. If provincial funding does not rise by an equal percentage, the burden of explanation will then be on the provinces. The bill simply removes the revenue guarantee, as it now stands. The amendment which I am proposing uses the revenue guarantee as a carrot to get something of real value for the programs, time for serious negotiations and moral pressure for provincial spending commitments while negotiations go on.
If the Liberal backbench members who expressed concern do not vote according to the logic of their arguments, we can only conclude that their real motive is that of the Minister of Finance, a motive which the minister explained to us in committee with, I may say, refreshing candour-that he would not support this amendment because it would cost him $2 billion over the next two years. That was his only explanation; it was going to cost him $2 billion. He believes that he can spend that money better elsewhere than on post-secondary education and health care costs.
We do not believe the government can spend that great amount of money, $2 billion, on better programs than postsecondary education and health care costs. Neither does the party to my left, the New Democratic Party. They do not believe it could be better spent elsewhere. Nor does the Economic Council of Canada. Nor does the Business Council on National Issues. Nor does The Canadian Council on Social Development. Nor did the all-party task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. All of them recommended against cutbacks in post-secondary education and health care costs. We hope that enough members on the other side will have the wisdom and the courage to join that illustrious company I just mentioned to ensure the passage of this amendment.

What I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, is that they could be grouped for debate but voted on separately.
April 1, 1982

Therefore 1 move:
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-97, to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977 and to provide for payments to certain provinces, be amended in Clause 6 by striking out lines 35 to 42 at page 11 and substituting the following therefor:
"(a) the aggregate of
(i)	$15.26 and
(ii)	the quotient obtained by dividing
(A)	the federal contribution payable for all the established programs to
all the provinces for the fiscal year commencing on April 1, 1975
by
(B)	the population of all the provinces for that fiscal year".
The effect of this amendment would be to restore for the duration of the next five-year fiscal period the money associated with the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee. It is similar to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) in so far as the amendment moved by the hon. member would leave the same amount of money but only for the next two years. As expressed by the hon. member, she would like to see that two years become a time for negotiation between the federal and provincial governments as to the role that the federal government plays in post-secondary education and national standards for health care.
We support the amendment of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands but we would like to see the money continued for the whole term. We are not against the two-year negotiating period but, as has always been our position, the money associated with the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee is money for health care and postsecondary education. It was regarded as such in the last fiscal arrangement and should continue to be regarded as such for the next five years.
There has been much confusion and debate about what has been known as the revenue guarantee. This is not the last time 1 will mention the guarantee because in all probability I will try to explain it again at third reading. In any event, I will try once again to explain for the record the way in which the government has been dishonest about the role of the revenue guarantee in the established programs financing.
I would like to begin by saying that there is no revenue guarantee at this time. There is nothing known, labelled or to be found in any piece of legislation as a revenue guarantee. For this reason I keep repeating that when I refer to the revenue guarantee I mean the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee, because that is really what we are talking about.
It is due to linguistic laziness that people refer to it as the revenue guarantee. It has become a dangerous habit because this conveys the notion that there is something called the revenue guarantee and therefore something separate from the established programs financing that the government can remove without being accused of taking away money intended for health care and post-secondary education.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
The fact of the matter is that the revenue guarantee, as such, ended in 1977. It was an agreement made in 1972 by the federal and provincial governments to compensate the provinces for whatever revenue they might lose as a result of the tax reform initiated in 1972. This agreement expired in 1977. At the same time that it expired, the federal government and the provinces were renegotiating the EPF and the funding for health care and post-secondary education, moving into a block funding system for those two programs. I assume that during other independent negotiations the provinces were complaining about the termination of the revenue guarantee. The federal government indicated that the revenue guarantee was finished, but since the provinces were unhappy about this fact, it would contribute extra money-$7.63 per capita, to be exact, plus one tax point-to the established programs financing. In other words, it offered to sweeten the pot.
On this condition the government asked the provinces if they would agree to integrate all the legislation into the new established programs financing bill rather than wait until 1980 for the hospital legislation to terminate. The provinces agreed to this and the revenue guarantee ended. The sum associated with compensation for termination of the revenue guarantee was rolled into the established programs financing.
What ensued was that the federal government consistently-up until the November, 1981 budget-regarded all the money in the established programs financing, including the money that the provinces were acquiring as a result of the tax point transfers, the money associated with the compensation for the termination of revenue guarantee, the cash payments, the transitional payments; all this money was regarded by ministers of the Liberal government as money for health care and post-secondary education. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in particular travelled across the country telling people what the percentage of federal government spending on health care and post-secondary education was and claiming great credit for spending this amount of money.
What occurred next was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) decided that he would like to solve his deficit problems, and although these problems do not result from these programs, he decided to pass on some of his deficits to the provinces and make the terrible mistake of trying to fight economic problems which were caused by other sources at the expense of these particular programs. The minister decided to change the government's perception of the money associated with the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee.
In committee this morning, the Minister of National Health and Welfare admitted that she wanted the provinces to regard the money associated with the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee as money to be spent on health care. If there is anything beneficial about meetings being held one after the other, it is that by sheer persistence you can sometimes get people to say something that they have been desperately trying to avoid saying for a number of days. In any

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
event, she said she regarded that money in that way but could not persuade the provinces.
1 have admitted all along that the provinces were wrong about this. They made a very serious mistake in the first few years of that last agreement, which was a very good agreement for them. They should have said, "Yes, all that money is for health care and post-secondary education", and they should have gone ahead and spent all that money on health care and post-secondary education. If they had done that, they would not be in the spot they are in today. They would not be in that spot if they had not let their percentage spending fall. They were partly to blame too.
Elowever, the federal government, particularly the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as she admitted this morning, regarded that money as money for health care and postsecondary education. What has the government done? It seems the Minister of Finance has said, "I want to save money anyway, so here is a good angle: we will throw the arguments of the provincial governments back in their faces and keep repeating them to them". That is what the federal government has been doing. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, probably embarrassed-initially, at least-by the cutbacks in this particular area, has tried to claim that she always had this view of the revenue guarantee; but this morning it seemed to me she slipped up for a minute and indicated that yes, she had seen this money spent this way, and she wished the provinces had spent it on health care and post-secondary education, but they did not. She could not persuade them, so now the federal governement is going to take it away from the provinces.
My position is that the federal government was right all along. It was right until it changed its mind in November of 1981. It should have stuck to its position. It should have stayed with the amount of support it regarded as necessary to provide for health care and post-secondary education and entered this new period of negotiating national health standards with that amount of money in its hand. It should have said, "We want to give this much support to health care and post-secondary education, we want to continue to give this much support to health care and post-secondary education and we want to give it under the following conditions". That would have been a much stronger bargaining position for the federal government had it entered this new negotiating period in that way. But instead, what has the federal government done? It wants to bargain for tougher national health care standards, but it is taking money off the table, and this is more unfortunate than I can possibly express. It does not bode well for the negotiations I want the federal government to go into. I am not taking the side of many of the provinces which say that the federal government should stay out of medicare, that it should not have an opinion about how this money should be spent and that it should not demand accountability. I want the federal government to do all those things. My complaint about this legislation is that it makes it more difficult for the federal government to do that. There was really no need for it to do
this. This is a stupid, blind move which does not have to be made. The federal government could move into these negotiations with all the money it was previously giving to health care and post-secondary education with a strong commitment to both those programs and have much more success at the negotiating table than it has now. Our amendment is designed to put that money back in.
All the groups which appeared before us in the committee and everyone I can think of, except the Liberal Party, have the same view of the consequences of the cutbacks I have just enunciated. The Canadian Health Coalition, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, The Canadian Council on Social Development-it did not matter who it was; all the witnesses before the committee took the view that it would be very damaging indeed for the federal government to go ahead with these cutbacks.
Our health care system is in a crisis. I do not like to use the word "crisis" over and over again because it is a word that is used too much in this House, and certainly our health care system could be a lot worse.

speechtext:
I am reluctant to use the word "crisis", but generally things do not just deteriorate overnight. It is a process, and I think this step by the government is one significant step in that process. It is not the end of the world, but this step makes it unlikely that in another area-that is, the negotiation of standards and conditions and the clarification and enforcement of those conditions-negotiations will succeed in the way I know most Canadians would want them to succeed and in the way I know my own party wants them to succeed. This is just another step down the road to a time when some provinces in particular-but all provinces-will feel the bite of these cutbacks.
The responses of the various provinces will differ because the medicare systems in the provinces differ. However, the consequences will be similar, as I have said, in terms of there being an effect by the cutbacks. However, I am particularly concerned about provinces like Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. I pick these three provinces by virtue of the fact that they are the three provinces which still charge premiums for medicare. This says something about how they like to finance medicare. They do not like to finance medicare in as progressive a way as possible. They are more attached than other provinces to "user-pays" views of health care.

speechtext:
I am told it is the same in Yukon. We did find that when we went up to Yukon. When the federal-provincial task force went up to Yukon, we found that in spite of all the rhetoric of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, at hospitals in the Territories for which she is responsible they were imposing user fees. I think that got out and they were
April 1, 1982

discontinued shortly thereafter, but sometimes there is a difference between appearance and reality.
As 1 was saying, in some provinces in particular, there will be a move to reintroduce and strengthen some of the private funding mechanisms that are already there. Some provinces will be looking for more ways to bring private money in to compensate for the lack of public money. In some cases this will be welcomed by these provinces.
Medicare is not as established in the national fabric as we all like to think it is. Any program which is only 18 years old is not very established. In the long run of political history a program of 18 years' duration is not very established at all. Medicare is a very young and fragile political fact. Many of the people who were so violently opposed to medicare only 18 years ago are not dead yet, they are still around. They still hold grudges. Perhaps they would still like not to have medicare. We have to be very careful that we do not provide the political pretext for all these people to come out of the woodwork again. They have been lying low while there has been a lot of money around. We can have almost any system we like if there is a lot of money to spread around, but when we come across hard economic times and we create the political context and economic context for medicare that the Minister of Finance is helping to create now, these people will start to show up again, and the arguments for more private money in the system will start to show up again. They will show up, ironically, in some of the provinces which have the most money and the most ability to fund their medicare systems in a progressive way entirely from general revenues.
It has always seemed to me to be a complete mystery why provinces like Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia cannot afford to fund their medicare systems out of general revenues through a progressive taxation system, when Manitoba, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick can afford to do this. Why? Because there is still that philosophical hostility to medicare which exists in certain places more strongly than in others.

Medicare is not just a matter of money; it is also a matter of commitment to a particular view of society and of the Canadian community as a place where people ought to have available high quality health care, whether they are rich or poor, whether they live in the Atlantic provinces or in Toronto. Medicare embodies a particular view of the country. It is a universal program which is available to people because they are Canadians, not because they are poor or have passed some
Federal Transfers to Provinces
kind of test. This is something we want to say about Canada. People in Canada, unlike those in many other countries-and the United States comes to mind-do not have to worry about the financial consequences of becoming sick. If they feel that there might be something wrong with them, there is no disincentive to attending doctors' offices for early diagnosis. They do not have to put it off until family allowance cheques come in or until they can afford it next week because they would like to buy bicycles for their children.
For most Canadians medicare is a classic example of what co-operative federalism can be when it is made to work and when it is informed by the kind of vision about which I have been talking. I think the Minister of Finance and the government are making a mistake; they will rue the day. I do not want to be standing around here or somewhere else down the road saying "I told you so." I would much rather the government accepted either the Tory amendment or ours and give time to conduct the policy discussion first in order to discover what kinds of medicare and post-secondary systems Canadians want. Then the fiscal decisions can be made afterwards. As The Canadian Council on Social Development pointed out, it is being done totally backwards. They are making fiscal decisions first and then deciding on what kind of system Canadians want. In that event, as has happened many times before, the financial structures will determine the system we get rather than the system determining the financial structures.
I hope these amendments will pass, and that Liberal members will have a change of heart and vote for them.

There has been much said about it, but we have not seen any evidence.
1 should like to take a look at the numbers themselves, at the evidence. Hon. members know that on March 19 the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) released a statement in which he gave some important figures. The first and most important part of the statement was the total number of dollars involved. Over the past five years, under both equalization and established programs financing, we spent approxiamtely $61 billion. Over the next five years we will spend $105 billion. We are spending $16.4 billion this year, and that will rise in 1986-87 to a total of $26.3 billion. Out of that, we see that the federal government will spend some $76.2 billion on health care and on post-secondary education. This year-$11.6 billion will go to those two categories, and in 1986-87 it will be $19.2 billion. We are talking about huge amounts of money and about very respectable rates of growth in our transfers to the provinces. We are not talking about cutbacks-or abandoning our responsibilities. We are talking about a reasonable maintenance of the standards and dedication of the government to these two vital programs.
1 think we should look at the fact that the growth here parallels the growth in the economy. It is a reasonable, planned growth and an amount the economy can manage. It is not unlimited growth; it is not a flat line, either. We are seeing approximate 12 per cent increases year after year over the next five years. Can we be satisfied that this growth rate is adequate?
I refer the House to the statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) yesterday, from which I will quote directly:
It is no secret that we are in a time of economic restraint. But the federal government is committed to upholding its side of the bargain when it comes to financing social programs for Canadians. We will not reduce our support for health care. In fact, over the next five years federal contributions for health will increase at an average annual rate of 13.4 per cent. Next year our support will grow by 12.2 per cent. The federal contribution to the provinces for health will total about $8.5 billion next year. This translates to a total of $347 for each person living in Canada.
As the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated, that is a very respectable maintenance and growth level for the health care program. When the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) appeared before the committee, he made the same kinds of commitments. We are not abandoning our responsibilities; we are maintaining and expanding them responsibly.
Also we must ask ourselves why we have not supported the two amendments which have been put forward. The Minister of National Health and Welfare gave the answer in the first sentence which I quoted:
It is no secret that we are in a time of economic restraint.

We simply do not believe that we are sacrificing the quality of the programs by not spending that money, and we do not believe that those expenditures are called for during this period of restraint.
A very great deal has been made about the $5.7 billion that somehow has magically been taken out of this whole program. This amount, called by the opposition the revenue guarantee, for the next five years would not have gone to health care or post-secondary education. The premiers have told us that. They told us last August that they would not spend this money on those programs. They do not automatically consider this money to be committed to those programs. They consider this money to be simply a transfer from the federal treasury to the provincial treasuries. This is money to be spent at their discretion. Perhaps by chance it could go to health care or postsecondary education. Equally by chance, it could be spent on highways, on sewers or on some other physical development of assets within the provinces. Their choice would be to spend the money as they see fit on their own provincial priorities. There were to be no guarantees that this money would be dedicated to those programs.
It is fallacious to argue that we are reducing our funding for these social programs by that amount simply because that amount is not in our budget. There was no guarantee in the beginning that the amount would be spent on those programs.
I believe restraint is needed. We have all received that message. What are we restraining here? We are not saying to the Canadian people that we are cutting back on funding to universities, to hospital care and medical care. We are not saying that. The figures 1 quoted earlier indicate the commitment we have to sustain these institutions and these programs. What we are saying instead is that the sky is not the limit. We cannot take that approach today. We simply have to put a cap on the rate of growth. We have to say that a reasonable expansion that takes into account the expansion in the economy will be permitted. We will not permit unlimited spending increases. We have to put a cap on those. We have to watch our spending as we heard so eloquently today and yesterday from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and as we have heard from the Secretary of State who spoke yesterday in the committee. We have heard the commitments of these ministers to quality in these programs.
Anyone who wants to find out the direction of our spending programs and our commitments for the next five years would be well advised to review the notes of the committee hearings. The debate was stimulating. Both ministers very clearly stated their personal beliefs and commitments to these programs. They have each indicated they are allowing their spending to expand to protect existing programs. They do not intend to go for new programs or for unlimited new increases in spending. The Canadian people do not want that. We have a commitment to Canadians to restrain our spending to within the growth limit of our economy. We are maintaining that commitment in this bill.
April 1, 1982

1 do not think anyone in our party has to apologize for restraining increases in spending for medical care, for hospitalization or for post-secondary education. Members of this government are the people who originally urged the beginnings of these programs. Ours is the government that put these programs into place. Ours is the government that has defended these programs. Ours is the government, as we have seen, that will nurture these programs over the coming five years. We make no apologies either for our commitment to these programs or for our commitment to restrain our spending.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to participate in the debate concerning Bill C-97. 1 wish to address my comments to, and focus on the amendment that has been introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald).
I was interested in the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) and his recognition that there will be a cut of SI billion a year. I was interested to know about his commitments to quality, yet he believes that quality somehow can come without any expenditure. I am interested in those comments because it reminds me of the person who makes a commitment to a loved one and writes a note saying: "1 want to see you more than anything else; 1 am coming to visit you tonight". Then there is a postscript to the note: "I will be over if it does not rain." The commitment which the parliamentary secretary outlines is not a commitment to philosophy. He also says, "do not confuse us with the details as to how we will deal with it."
The terms of the amendment put forward by my colleague allow the federal government a way out of the federal-provincial impasse which has unfortunately obscured the very serious problems faced by Canada's post-secondary education community. It is in this area that I wish to focus my remarks.
Regrettably, this piece of legislation both begins and ends any opportunity to pull together the potential contributions of both those levels of government. Instead, it does little more than add to the current state of unproductive confrontation between levels of government and the disquiet in our advanced educational institutions. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is a selfevident rule of policy formulation that this bill is coming at the wrong end of the process. First, we should have had public hearings that would have involved all the interested parties in the nation's post-secondary community. Then on that basis, the federal and provincial government should have sat down and worked out negotiated funding mechanisms, grounded in mutually satisfactory visions of the role of post-secondary education in Canada's future. Then, and only then, should those agreements have been enshrined in federal legislation.
The current Secretary of State takes every opportunity to make the point that the support of post-secondary education has already been studied enough. Indeed, the important contributions of the special task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements have taken the country well down the road to informed decision making. However, we should not forget the limited terms of reference of the parliamentary task force.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
As reported in Hansard for February 5, 1981, we find the following:
-to examine the programs authorized by the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, focusing in particular on fiscal equalization, the tax collection agreements, the Canada Assistance Plan, and Established Programs Financing; and that this examination take place within the context of the government's expenditure plan as set out in the October 18, 1980, budget.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the task force was not empowered to address itself to non-financial matters, this is in keeping with this government's insistence that the future direction of post-secondary education is entirely a matter of dollars and cents agreements with the provincial governments. Is it any wonder that such unilateral actions as the federal government has taken with Bill C-97 have caused the students, staff, faculties and administrators, who are committed to an increased vitality in the post-secondary community, to suspect the motives of this government? Where is this government's umbrella statement of the future place of post-secondary education in Canadian society? It runs surveys and polls in a variety of other areas, but it does not survey opinion in this area; rather, it attempts to dictate it. It does not formulate long-term policies; rather, it counts its short-term spending visibility as most important. It has no vision, merely the desire for political credit.
In my riding of Waterloo three prominent national postsecondary institutions, the University of Waterloo, Wilfrid Laurier University and Conestoga College of Applied Arts & Technology, met to discuss what they called the crisis in postsecondary education. The message communicated to me in that public meeting was that these institutions feel like a basketball being bounced back and forth between two levels of government. They also voiced considerable support for the Canadian Association of University Teachers' proposal to extend existing EPF agreements for two years in return for a provincial commitment to increase post-secondary spending by 11.7 per cent in 1982-83 and 11.9 per cent in 1983-84. They have proposed that the two-year cooling off period be used for a joint inquiry to be conducted by the federal government and the Council of Ministers of Education. Open, public hearings would be held so that students, faculty, staff, administrators and community leaders could express their respective wants and needs in the area of advanced learning. The inquiry would be given only one year to report its findings, and the second year would be devoted to federal-provincial negotiations on the basis of those findings.
That is what I mean by pulling together a Canadian vision for the future role of post-secondary education and its support. A practical, creative mechanism for negotiated change. That, Mr. Speaker, is the process for which our party's amendment provides.
Lest members opposite scoff at the potential utility of such a policy-formulation process, let me relate it to the work of the federal cultural policy review committee, sometimes referred

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
to as the Applebaum-Hebert commission. Its recently submitted "Summary of Briefs and Hearings" casts an interesting light indeed on the need for a similar investigation into the future of post-secondary education in Canada. The chapter entitled "Knowledge and Scholarship" deals with the relationship of knowledge and scholarship to culture and federal cultural policy. The brief submitted by the Canadian Teachers' Federation zeros in on the policy vacuum which I address here today in the context of this amendment. It says:
The problem of cultural choice cannot, in our view, be divorced from the question of educational policy. The need for a coherent cultural policy is an aspect of the need for a national consensus on educational goals.
The Canadian Association of University Teachers made a detailed response on this theme. They said:
It is ill advised and unrealistic to try to devise an adequate national cultural policy without discussing the role and development of education. Taken as a whole, the education system:
1.	provides the knowledge and intellectual base on culture;
2.	acts as the most important institution for the transmission of our cultural
heritage to future citizens;
3.	plays a direct role in the training of future arts and cultural thinkers; and
4.	increasingly provides important facilities and resources for cultural events
accessible to the general public.
The Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council made a point which goes to the very heart of the bill before us today. They said:
The human sciences, in applying a reasoned approach to the perception and assessment of human materials and events, attempt to place current problems in the perspective of things past and to vistas on the future in the light of lasting human values.
Very telling, that phrase "lasting human values". In view of our discussion here today, Mr. Speaker, I wish that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) had the wisdom and political energy to have grounded Bill C-97 in any recognizable "lasting human values".
I do not want to overdraw my comparison between the need for a full review of post-secondary education policy, such as it exists, and the federal cultural policy review initiated by the then secretary of state, the Hon. David MacDonald, in November, 1979, so I will conclude my remarks on it with this quotation from the brief presented by the Association of Universities & Colleges of Canada. They said:
Be it fundamental or applied, humanistic, social or scientific, university based or not, research is directed at the creation of new knowledge and of new understanding of ourselves and our world. It is intellectual and creative activity at its best, and it is essential for the cultural advancement of society.
The point as I see it, Mr. Speaker, is that without first laying out its vision of the role of post-secondary education, the federal government risks permanent-albeit unintended- damage to the cutting edge of Canadian intellectual activity in generations yet to come.
What, pray tell, has possessed this government to take such a scatter-gun or, one might say, scatter-brain approach to the funding of advanced learning as that documented in this legislation before us today? Why have they not first come to some informed decisions about general policy directions? Just what do the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State
imagine will be the consequences of this sort of unilateral action? What have they envisioned to be the role of community colleges and universities? Given the underfunding, which the parliamentary secretary has just recognized, enshrined in Bill C-97, what do they expect post-secondary institutions to look like in two, Five or ten years? Will they have libraries, for example? What quality of education will they be able to offer? Will our best scholars in areas other than Canadian studies or job-creating areas have fled the country? To what social groups are they directing educational opportunities? How many of the present institutions will be left in existence?
These are just some of the questions which need to be answered. At the same time they must be considered against the background of the final report of the task force entitled, "Fiscal Federalism in Canada", to the effect that any further cuts forced on post-secondary institutions will be cutting not into fat, but into sinew and marrow. The Secretary of State's predecessor concluded his testimony to that task force by:
-noting the need for a federal strategy that will address the challenges facing the post-secondary system in the eighties, a federal strategy that will actively support the achievement of national objectives, and a federal strategy that is realistic in light of fiscal restraint and that is consistent with basic principles such as accountability and visibility.
While I have yet to see an adequate definition-to say nothing of a social justification-for "visibility", I am close to agreeing with the balance of his remarks. What concerns me most, however, is that there has been no new initiative from the federal government to follow up on those bare thoughts since they were delivered in June of last year. In the absence of such a policy framework from the Secretary of State, we are faced with the financial ultimatum contained in Bill C-97. This is not good enough to encourage the wholehearted cooperation of those in the post-secondary community in terms of the future.
The amendment, which I support and which I encourage this House to consider and support, seeks to provide a mechanism for the discussion of these important aspects of the funding of post-secondary institutions.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is, once more, a pleasure to take part in the debate on fiscal arrangements this time at the report stage. 1 believe that the two amendments, we are now discussing, one by the member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and one by the member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), would both have the effect of delaying or extending established programs financing as it is now, including the revenue guarantee. At least, aside from all the statutory complexities or technical amendments, that would be the effect of the amendment by the member for Kingston and the Islands. Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize, and I repeat what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said earlier, that revenue guarantee is a program that was introduced in 1972 to protect the provinces against drastic changes in the federal tax base. The
April 1, 1982

House will recall that in 1971 it legislated a thorough reform of the tax system and, at the time, some provinces said that this would drastically change the federal tax base.
Since at least nine provinces-all the provinces with the exception of Quebec, which has its own system for collecting income tax-are using the federal tax base to establish their own provincial tax, any change in the federal tax base also affects provincial revenues. The provinces have said: Give us a guarantee that the drastic reform you are now introducing will not just as drastically reduce the revenues of the provinces. The guarantee was what is still known as the revenue guarantee program. In fact, the program was extended in 1977, when the federal government and the provinces were negotiating agreements on block funding to replace the former shared-cost programs.
The question is, therefore, whether or not the revenue guarantee the government now proposes to eliminate was actually a part of programs financing. In 1977, the federal government or rather Parliament, decided that for administrative purposes, including the sending out of cheques, payments under the guaranteed revenue program, according to legislation that still exists today, would be made by the ministers responsible for the programs at the federal level in the same proportions as financing for health programs and post-secondary education. So that is the issue. In the report by the Standing Committee on Fiscal Arrangements mentioned earlier in the House this afternoon, a detailed history is given of the revenue guarantee program and various interpretations are given. In the tables listing the payments, revenue guarantee is listed separately from the programs, but there was a recommendation, which J supported at the time, that the revenue guarantee program should be allocated to the programs. And that is the big difference between the recommendation by the Parliamentary task force and the government's proposals. It is one of the big differences.
Now, is that justified? That is the question. Is it justified in terms of political morality and political judgment? Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that the provincial premiers published their press release in August, after the task force completed its report. We did not know they were going to say that. Our report was not published until August 31, but for all practical purposes, it was completed in terms of political decision making around July 24 or 25. The provincial premiers said that they did not consider the revenue guarantee as being allocated to programs financing. 1 am sorry about this, because I would have preferred to see the money allocated to the programs, and that could probably be justified. However, one of my reasons for supporting the position of the government today is, that despite the recommendations I agreed to in order to reach a political consensus on this matter, I have always believed that revenue guarantee was not an equitable transfer. I see the member for Mississauga-South (Mr. Blenkarn) is smiling. 1 have always thought the program was unfair, because it was an automatic transfer of funds, no strings
Federal Transfers to Provinces
attached, to all provinces, while the only program we have traditionally said would be entirely discretionary and automatic is the fiscal equalization program.
Mr. Speaker, there is justification for this, and for more than one reason. Even if the program were eliminated, we must remember that because of the changes proposed in the November budget which will result in an increase in the federal tax base, automatically, the provinces, if in some cases they introduce legislation to adjust to changes in the federal budget in most provinces this is done automatically, at least as far as personal income tax is concerned they will benefit from nearly $685 million in additional revenue. The members opposite claim this does not count, because these are provincial revenues the provinces themselves collect in the form of taxes, which is true. The fact remains, however, that it is a case of political judgment. We have to make a decision in terms of political morality, and the decision is up to the elected politicians. When the federal government makes a decision in Parliament, and Parliament legislates an increase in the federal tax base which provides additional revenue for the provinces, then, even if these are provincial revenues, at least we should consider the fact that such action, both political and parliamentary, to some extent justifies eliminating a program such as the revenue guarantee, which the provinces themselves decided they were not going to allocate to the other programs. Mr. Speaker, there is another side to this question. In the final analysis, when I add up the figures-

When I add up the figures, it is obvious what the over-all effect will be, even putting aside the question of additional revenues, caused by increases in the federal tax base. Hon. members of the opposition say that we should not count them. However, even if we do not count them, the over-all effect of the arrangement being proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the arrangement that he made with the Atlantic provinces, just considering the increases to the equalization program, will be to more than compensate the provinces which receive equalization for the losses attributable to, or caused by, the elimination of the revenue guarantee.

That is $60-odd million over and above the increase that the province of New Brunswick will receive in equalization payments. The over-all effect of these changes will be that only those provinces that do not receive equalization will be affected even when we do not count the increase in provincial revenues due to the enlargement of the federal tax base. I say that in terms of political morality you can count them, but even if you do not count them the over-all effect of
this will be that only the provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta will be affected to any significant degree. The equalization recipient provinces will be very generously compensated due to the changes in the equalization program.
I know there will be different political opinions. All the provincial governments will continue to say that there are federal cutbacks. That is the nature of the political game. They have to bargain, to negotiate hard, particularly at this time because the unions are asking for increases in wages. Some 80 per cent of what they are talking about that goes into postsecondary education and health care is wages. It is a tough period, they have to take a tough stand and it is good politics to blame the federal government. I expect that to continue. But the facts are that the over-all increases in revenue to the provinces that receive equalization will more than offset any loss due to the ending of the revenue guarantee. It will more than compensate them. If the provinces decide that they want to squeeze the post-secondary institutions, or the hospitals, or the doctors, or anybody else, that is a political judgment that they are making. It is totally untrue and a distortion to say that it will be because of federal cutbacks. I repeat that I have not included, in making that judgment, those revenues that will be automatically provided by the enlargement of federal tax base.
Let us consider another thing, if anyone wants to talk about what is fair and what is unfair in politics. In the last five years, in the arrangement that finished at midnight yesterday the federal contribution has represented a larger percentage of the total expenditure from year to year. For example, in my province, New Brunswick, in post-secondary education contribution, if you include second language and minority language education programs, the yearly average has been an 18.4 per cent increase. The provincial government only allocated 11.5 per cent. We provided for that. If we had a system that permitted the provinces not to allocate the same amount that they were receiving from the federal government, what is so bad about that if there is going to be some adjustment on that in the future?
1 quoted in the House of Commons ten days ago that in 1981-82 for example, the fiscal year that ended yesterday, the federal contribution to post-secondary education and second language education programs in New Brunswick represents 107 per cent of what the province spent. The federal contribution represents 99 per cent of what the institutions spent. That means that the legislature of New Brunswick, through the New Brunswick government, allocates only 1 per cent of what is spent in that province on education after high school.
I recognize, and I did recognize in the House of Commons when I quoted those figures, that one cannot expect the Atlantic provinces to be able to sustain, on their own, postsecondary education systems. First of all, we cannot afford it. Secondly, too many of our young people, once they have graduated, go elsewhere because of the needs of the economy elsewhere. So why should there be a sacrifice by the taxpayers
April 1, 1982

of these provinces to train people so that they can go and work in Alberta or Ontario? So it is justifiable to spend a higher percentage in the Atlantic provinces. All the arrangements since 1966 recognize that. There was a special arrangement made in 1966-67 also.
However, in 1976-77 in my province the federal contribution was only 76 per cent or 78 per cent; now it is 107 per cent of what the province spends. Anyone who has sense and who wants to be fair ought to admit that this is not normal, that there is no reason why the provincial government should receive 7 per cent more than what it spends on post-secondary education. The equalization program provides unconditional support but it is totally unjustifiable to make a profit on program transfers.
