Emergency Planning
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all correspondence, notes, minutes of meetings, memos, telegrams and communications relating to the order respecting Emergency Planning, P.C. 1981-1305, May 21, 1981, Registration SI/81-76 June 10, 1981.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was last in the House, I had just made a brief five-minute introductory speech before time ran out. Therefore, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to continue my remarks.
From time to time in this House non-issue issues seem to dominate its deliberations and the media outside this chamber. These non-issue issues, as I call them, are issues that really have little or no substance to them, but they are issues that pack an enormous psychological clout. They are designed for that very reason, to scare the heck out of as many Canadians as possible and, in so doing, besmirch the reputation of the present administration.
We have had excellent examples of two of these non-issue issues over the last six months. The two issues that I refer to are, of course, the taxation of imputed rental value of homes which the official opposition party raised, and the issue of internment camps created by planning order P.C. 1981-1305.
If I had the opportunity of speaking to the first non-issue issue, I would bring the attention of the House to its inadequacy. However, since we are dealing with the second one, it is my pleasure this afternoon to outline the nature of that issue, as I see it, and explain frankly why Canadians should not be concerned with that as an issue and why it should be completely dismissed and taken from the table of legitimate debate in Canadian society today.
We have two choices in this House when it comes to emergency planning. We can believe that we are living in a paradise in which nothing happens, to which nothing can happen and for which there is no need to plan; or we can believe that since we live in a very real world with all sorts of potential dangers in it which are growing increasingly more hazardous as we move more steadily into the industrial nuclear age, we must prepare for one emergency or another, domestic or foreign.
This government chose the latter option. I do not think anyone in this House would dispute that. Any party that forms the government would have to assume that at some time or other, in one part of the country or other, emergencies will develop, that we must anticipate them and have the personnel, resources and equipment ready to deal with them. If you accept that we must be ready for those unknown, unforeseen and yet very real emergencies that lie ahead of us, and we must obviously plan for them.
This government was faced with two basic options. It could have decided to plan exclusively within the confines of one single, large federal department. I am sure members opposite

April 1, 1982
Emergency Planning
would argue that such a department would be typically and bureaucratically top-heavy, and in the end when it had to act would probably do so in a way less effective than we had anticipated.
The other option, of course, was to have built on the diversity which characterizes the Canadian nation, the diversity which hon. members opposite often referred to in many of the debates on the Constitution. This diversity I am referring to is the diversity of resources that lie in the volunteer section of our society, at the provincial level and at the municipal level. The federal government's relationship to those three segments would be to provide the resources necessary for each of those three groups to do whatever job is needed in that future unforeseen circumstance of national, regional or local tragedy.
Of those two options which I have just outlined, the government in its wisdom, and I hope members opposite will agree, has chosen to create plans built on the diversity of talent which exists in this nation today. So far 1 do not think I have said anything with which members opposite could disagree. The conclusions which this government has reached, namely that we should have emergency plans and they should be based on the diversity of Canada, would, I think, meet with the agreement of all three parties in this chamber.
Having said that, and I think having the agreement of members opposite, we now begin to enter the realm of speculation and, 1 would argue, distortion by the official opposition. It claims that in planning for these future emergencies, this government has created new, unprecedented powers. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has made that claim time and time again. The Globe and Mail, which appears to be his official organ, has repeated that claim almost as often as he has.
That accusation is, simply, straightforwardly and patently false. I dare not call it a lie because that would be unparliamentary language. But it is a distortion of the reality of the planning authority which is the backbone of this planning order. The planning order does not create new powers. What it does is assign responsibilities to the various departments of government. These departments have always had those responsibilities. There is nothing new in any of them. Those responsibilities stretch all the way back to the administration of the late Lester B. Pearson. Those responsibilities are almost two decades old.
The disturbing aspect of this debate, the distortion which has been made by the opposition party, is that the opposition knows this. It knows that those responsibilities have always been with those departments. It knows this because members of the opposition recently asked for a legal opinion on that very issue. The opinion which they received concluded that the government had the power to issue such an order in council as I am presently describing and that the government has acted validly and within an existing jurisdiction.
Being aware of that legal opinion, opposition members have apparently shifted the focus of their argument. They have moved on to ask this question: If the departments already have responsibility for that planning, do they have the authority to implement the plans? I believe the answer to that is twofold. First, the answer may be found in existing legislation. I would point out to hon. members opposite that the National Defence Act provides military aid to the civil power. The Energy Supplies Emergency Act of 1979 carries within it the authority to implement emergency plans, as do the various plans that fall under the aegis of the disaster financial assistance arrangements.
Although I could make further comments, I hope I have made my point that within existing legislation there lies a firm foundation of authority for the government to exercise and implement emergency plans which may be necessary in the future. There may be need for future special legislation to deal with areas which are not covered by the legislation which I have enumerated. It may be that special legislation will be prepared by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) who has special responsibility for these matters. I cannot speak on his behalf so I do not know if he will be bringing special legislation to the attention of the House.
It may that the House will wish to deal with special legislation at the time of an emergency. A decision such as that is not without risks. For example, it takes several days to prepare any bill for discussion and obtain passage in the House. In times of emergency we cannot afford a couple of days to await the reaction of federal, provincial and municipal governments. Reaction by these governments as well as volunteer groups such as the Red Cross must be immediate and focused. A couple of days just might mean the difference between life and death for thousands and perhaps millions of Canadians.
What happens if the House is not sitting? What happens if the House is in recess or has prorogued? Indeed, what happens if this House were dissolved and the three parties were involved in a general election? These are matters which every member of the House should recognize and remember when regarding, as suspiciously as opposition members do, the powers within the War Measures Act. Despite how abhorrent this act may appear to some members of the House, it allows the government to react immediately to any emergency which might arise when the House is not sitting. I would urge hon. members to recognize the attractive and responsible portions of that act and understand that it can be legitimately invoked on behalf of all Canadians at any time under conditions of a physical or military emergency.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that the major arguments and criticisms directed at this government over this non-issue issue, namely that it is without precedent, are totally false. 1 think I have demonstrated to the satisfaction of the House that there is absolutely nothing new or without precedent in the authority which this government would use to direct emergency operations within the dominion of Canada. Not only is there nothing new in this order, but more importantly it is obvious and clear that this order in council is within
April 1, 1982

the law. This government is not acting illegally and has absolutely nothing to hide.
The roots of this order lie deep in the administrative and legislative history of this House. They stand exposed: clearly, honestly and openly before all members in this chamber. For anyone opposite to conclude and argue otherwise is to give this debate an irrational and demeaning character which will not serve the interests and welfare of the citizens of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, prior to commencing my remarks I would like to ask for the indulgence of the House. 1 believe there are another fifteen minutes left before the government can make its summation and the mover, the member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Fries-en), can summarize as well. I wonder if the House would be so inclined as to give unanimous consent that 1 share those fifteen minutes with my colleague, the member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers)?
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, members of my party have not had an opportunity to express our views in this debate. I would like the opportunity to do so within the next fifteen minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There does not appear to be unanimous consent. I recognize the hon. member for Provencher.

That being the case, I regret that my colleague will not have an opportunity to speak. However, I intend to take the fifteen minutes.
With respect to the topic which is before us, the government emergency planning Order, I would first like to commend the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta for his vigilance, the vigilance of my deskmate, the member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), as well as that of other members in the House in terms of this planning order.
The member who spoke on behalf of the government a moment ago made it appear that this emergency planning order is simply a pro forma approach by the government. He said it is something the like of which the government has been in the practice of passing and that its justification is that it is good planning for the future. On the face of it, one might say there is some validity to those arguments; but are they the real issues which are facing us? 1 suggest that is not the case.
The issues facing us are the following. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta and other hon. members have mentioned them before. The first is why legislation was not brought into the House. Why did the government have to use a regulation, an order in council, to pass the emergency order? I telephoned a provincial member who participated at the federal-provincial conference and asked him if he and his colleagues agreed to this kind of procedure whereby this matter is dealt with through the regulatory approach. He said, "We raised objections even at that time", in terms of the scope
Emergency Planning
of these emergency planning orders. This is not a matter on which the government should be moving ahead and defending under the aegis of good planning. It goes much further than that.
It is interesting to note how quickly Canadians have become aware that their civil rights can be removed by the government, not through legislation but, rather, through this order. It is ironic that in this month when we will be getting back our Constitution, including a charter of rights, we should even be debating an emergency planning order by regulation rather than by legislation. Since the 1970 crisis, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has committed himself a number of times to bringing that kind of legislation to the House. It is because of the vigilance of hon. members on this side of the House, both in the House and outside, that this debate has been forced, and I commend those hon. members for that.
What is being defended by the government as being good planning? Let us look at some of the issues. I repeat that this planning order was never passed in the House or debated in the House other than through this motion. Under this planning order-without parliamentary approval, I might add-the Prime Minister could manage and co-ordinate the national information services. What are the national information services? Does this mean that freedom of the press will be suspended by a declaration, an edict or an order of the Prime Minister?
They do it in Russia.

Is that the national information service?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) could control and regulate farm production and food trade, both internal and external. Has that matter been debated with the farmers of Canada? Have they debated the fact that the Minister of Agriculture can control agricultural production and distribution?
When we discussed the Constitution we talked about mobility rights. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) would have the power under this order to control the registration and movement of civilian manpower and "arrange any required international manpower transactions".
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) could control all fuel production, assess national and regional requirements, establish such priorities as may be required and regulate international and external trade.
The next power to which I will refer is possibly the one which has been focused on most acutely in the public, and that is that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) would establish and operate civilian internment camps and, if necessary, by "the selective reduction and transfer of the present population". Those words need some interpretation.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: The RCMP are not involved either.
What does it mean? Are the RCMP involved?

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
No, they are not.

April 1, 1982
Emergency Planning

The minister has been asked in this House whether he is already working on the setting up of internment camps. He has been very coy in his answers because he does not want to answer definitively yes, that is what he is doing. However, if we follow the logic of the hon. member who just spoke-he said this is only for good planning-we wonder if this is being planned as well, and if it is not, is this then outside the scope of good planning? For example, the Solicitor General was asked recently whether he has already determined which prison population can be moved out so that civilian populations can be moved in. He chose not to answer that either.
People might say this is simply a scare tactic. If that charge is valid, why did the government not follow up on the commitment the Prime Minister has made since 1970 to bring legislation into this House? Why, in the stealth of night behind closed doors in cabinet, did a regulation have to be passed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Maybe it was in the stealth of day.
Surreptitiously.

No matter what time of day it was, it was wrong, and the reason hon. members opposite are back pedalling as rapidly as they can is that Canadians are very conscious of the fact that when their civil rights are in jeopardy, there will be a reaction. People will react against any government which appears to take powers unto itself which should be left to the people.
People might think we are over-reacting because "it can't happen in Canada".
Don't kid yourself!

Hon. members of this House have different backgrounds. I am not for a minute trying to equate this government with governments in other countries because I do not think that is a fair tactic. However, I want to put something before the House because someone has said that the only protection of civil rights is the constant vigilance of the electorate to maintain those rights. Why is it that Canadians who have ethnic backgrounds react so quickly to this kind of situation? They do so because they carry the scars of their own backgrounds. They carry the scars of bitter experiences in which governments have moved against people and the rights of those people. 1 want to tell the government very clearly that democratic rights can be removed very easily, and that can be seen to be very justifiable. However, a question remains as to whether the general public is willing to give up certain rights for the nebulous concept of immediate security. Many governments have sold the concept of restriction of civil rights for the illusory promise of security.
I said that many of us react because of our backgrounds. My own people, who were welcomed by this country, were able to escape, but some of our family members did not. My uncle, now passed on, spent 22 years in a Soviet internment camp. His crime? He was of the wrong political persuasion. What was that persuasion? He had never been involved in public life or political action. His crime was that he was a land owner. He
had property. It was not even his property, it was his father's, and because he was the eldest, he expected to inherit it. He felt he had a responsibility to his father to stay on that land, and he paid for it with 22 years of his life. His children, who happen to be my relatives, still cannot move back to the Crimea where the family once lived. They have never been back, and today they still live in Kazakhstan, in the so-called virgin lands, because of the crime of their father in that he was a land owner.
I am repeating myself because I do not want what 1 am saying to be equated with what this government or any Canadian government is doing. I am simply saying that all of us in the House must be vigilant and must not exchange supposed security for our rights. That is dangerous, extremely dangerous. The reason the government is in trouble on this issue is not necessarily to be found in all its provisions. The reason rather, is that the government chose again to act by order in council. The government did not see the need and definitely did not take the action of bringing the emergency order into the House in legislative form.
One must ask the question: how many times does the issue of government by regulation have to be expounded on the floor? When will the government learn that every time it does this it removes a little more of the rights of Canadians and of the responsibilities they have given to their representatives on this floor.
This issue is extremely critical in the minds of Canadians today because they are worried about their economic security. They are worried about the world scene in terms of a nuclear holocaust. They are convinced that they should not allow government to trample over their rights through orders in council and regulations for the supposed security and orderly planning which the government indicates is inherent in this emergency order. I commend the members of the House who have forced the government into debate through this mechanism. I regret that again legislation was not seen to be the best vehicle to bring the issue to the floor of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker-
April 1, 1982

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) rising on a point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am rising on a point of order so that the House will realize that the practice of a parliamentary secretary replying for a minister designated by the rules will not be taken as a precedent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair asked for unanimous consent of the House, recognizing that it was necessary, and there appeared to be unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There is in fact unanimous consent. I simply stated that this should not be taken as a precedent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for its consent.
1 assure the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) that we will not assume this to be a precedent. I am simply batting for the minister because unavoidably he is unable to be here.
I regret that this issue has aroused a number of unfortunate concerns in the minds of hon. members of the House and of Canadians as a whole. Some of the things which have been said really represent a misunderstanding. I do not question the intentions of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) or of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I think some of the statements which have been made are misleading. I do not think they are deliberately misleading but they are misleading. 1 should like to point out a couple of facts.
First, obviously the order in council cannot give government any powers it does not already have. It has been suggested today that the government is taking powers unto itself by virtue of this order in council. That is simply not correct. The order in council designates to various ministers the lines of jurisdiction to which they should be looking, in terms of the areas for which they are expected to have plans drawn up.
Second, it is very important to bear in mind that the order in council is not a brand new one. It is a revision of a 1965 order in council. 1 have read the 1965 order quite carefully. In fact there are previous orders going back to the 1940s, which I have also read quite carefully. They were not as comprehensive as the 1965 order in council. In the 1965 order there was reference to internment camps in wording identical to this one. It was delegated to the minister of justice in the 1965 order as opposed to the solicitor general, but it is in there; there is nothing new about it. What I am saying is that obviously the order was on the books the entire time the government, of which the hon. member for Provencher was a minister, was in power. If there was something in it which offended them about internment camps, they should have cancelled the order. But it was on the books the entire time they were in government. With regard to the internment camp issue, it would only come into force in the event of war. If Part I and Part II of the schedule are read carefully, that point can be quite clearly understood.
Reference was made today to vigilance on the part of the government and of the Canadian people. Can anyone seriously
Emergency Planning
suggest that the government would be living up to its obligations if it had no plans to deal with emergencies in the country? I would suggest not. It is incumbent upon the government to have in place plans to deal with certain emergencies which in fact could arise.
With regard to the motion before us today, is the government trying to hide anything? No, we are not trying to hide anything. We are agreeable to the motion. As hon. members know, we cannot table the documents until they have been translated. They are quite voluminous. Translation has been under way for some time but is not yet completed. I had discussions with other members of the House and the consensus was that we would be agreeable to an order which could be issued if the House gave its unanimous consent, indicating that the papers be tabled as soon as the translation is completed. If unanimous consent is not forthcoming on that, then we would vote for the motion. We have nothing to hide. Canadians have nothing to fear. This is good, sound planning with regard to possible emergencies-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen).

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I have no problem accepting the validity of the word of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith). I think he was sincere in saying that the government was willing to turn the papers over. However, I am not willing to accept the word of the PCO or the PMO on this, which I think is the greater concern. 1 put this motion to the House last fall. The government could have been getting these documents ready since then, if it were serious about it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is six months.

I put the motion on the floor because the government's argument has been that this is in preparation for an emergency. If in fact that is the case, the government could have begun with legislation out of which regulations would have flowed. The government has had plenty of time. As the parliamentary secretary said, the government has taken this from the 1965 order. I have read the 1965 order as well as this one. I would say with respect to the hon. member that this is not a simple redrafting. It is an entirely new order, if one makes a simple comparison between the 1965 order and this one.
If in fact there is no national emergency, then the government has time to bring forward legislation. If there is an emergency, then people have the right to know the nature of it, if the government really has trust in Canadians. There are some serious questions in the minds of Canadians, not the least of which rests upon a bedrock series of betrayals as the public sees it, from the leadership of the government. It is not simply this order which has betrayed the trust of Canadians; it is a long series of them. This is the culmination of those betrayals which the Canadian people feel.

April 1, 1982
Emergency Planning
I would add that it is the introduction of the new Constitution that raises questions. My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) would have liked to have spoken on this and asked what the effect of this order would be on Clause 11, subclause (g), of that new Constitution, which reads:
-not to be found guilty on account of any act or omission unless, at the time of the act, or omission, it constituted an offence under Canadian or international law-
Whatever that means. Are we now subject to international law? Subclause (g) continues:
-or was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations.
Just yesterday I raised an issue with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding Crown prerogative. What are the limits of Crown prerogative? The Prime Minister said to me here in the House, as reported in Hansard at page 16005, the following:
Certainly I am on sound ground in saying that any prerogative, royal or otherwise, can be limited by statute.
There is no statute, Mr. Speaker. Is that not saying that there is no limit to the Crown prerogative which the Prime Minister could invoke in times that he deems to be a matter of national emergency?
When the co-chairman of the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments wrote to the Prime Minister, the letter was redirected to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). That letter confirms the fact that Crown prerogative would have precedent over any other aspect of these provisions.
We have a choice in our country and that is whether we are going to be governed by man or by law. It has been the history of our land and all democratic societies that freedom rests upon law. The reality of Crown prerogative within the loose context of these provisions indicates that we are easily becoming the victims of rule by man. 1 hope we never come to the stage in our country where a man, under the provisions of this law-this order in council-has control over censorship, and has control over all the powers of information. Surely the public needs information in order to make decisions. The public can be easily swayed, and if we are going to be ruled by a man with both kinds of powers that 1 mentioned, then surely we are falling victims to the powers of a dictatorship.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, we were treated to the hon. member from Gloucester (Mr. Breau)-who was privileged to go around the country with the fiscal arrangements task force, its report being known as the Breau report-coming before the House and trying to justify what he said was political morality. He indicated that, despite the terms of that report, which clearly dealt with what is described now as revenue guarantee, he was prepared to sell that principle out. He was prepared to sell out the principle that the report sets out in Chapter X. 1 read the relevant parts of that chapter into the record on second reading. In political morality one must wonder about the attitude of the member for Gloucester, particularly when he compares the settlement eventually arrived at with his province. He says somewhere along the line "We lost, we lost a great deal of money on established programs; but we picked it up on equalization." The fact is, if he would read his own report-he was the chairman of the task force-with respect to equalization he would find that the province of New Brunswick was diddled out of equalization and is being diddled now,

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
with his concurrence and consent, with respect to the established programs financing act.
The only interpretation, Mr. Speaker, that can possibly be given to the member for Gloucester of his performance here this afternoon is that he is looking for a cabinet position. He is looking for a cabinet position and probably he is not going to get it. He is prepared to sell out his province, sell out his university, sell out the hospitals, because he thinks he is getting more for them under this deal than he would get if he stood behind his own report, a report to which he should be proud to attach his name. I and other members of the committee sat with him as our chairman, and we came up with a report that was virtually unanimous, saying very clearly and unequivocally that any cuts in the established programs would cut into muscle and sinew, and would make those programs not viable.
From time to time, Mr. Speaker, as it goes in political contest, when you have a member from one party representing one part of the city and a member from another party representing another part of the city, we often find we are in debate locally. So I want to make some reference to the speech made to the House this afternoon by the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher).
He was refreshingly honest. He made no bones about it. He said clearly that $937 million in cash is being taken from the provinces that would normally go to health and post-secondary education this year, and $1,058 million next year. He said quite clearly the government could not accept the amendment of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) because we are in a period of restraint. He said the government had no intention of spending that kind of money on post-secondary education and health care.
He was not refreshingly honest, unfortunately, with respect to the question of restraint. He followed the attitude expressed by the government in that respect, restraint in every program except the programs that mean most to the people of Canada. We see no restraint in the CBC. Their budget goes up by $73 million. We see no restraint in C1DA. Its budget goes up $146 million. We see no restraint on government advertising. We will have more programs with Canada geese flying across the TV screens. We see no restraint with regard to the programming for the forthcoming Royal visit. We see no restraint with the Enterprise Development Board which is blowing $125 million on Consolidated Computer. We see no restraint in the enterprise development loan guarantee program and the Enterprise Development Board. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) clearly admits this will cost us millions and millions of dollars as loans are defaulted on one after another because of inept, incompetent and incapable management.
We see no restraint with respect to guarantees under the Export Development Program, for example, guarantees to make 10 per cent or less money available to Algerians to build monuments to the revolution. One colleague suggests it was two bananas and a doughnut around it and a McDonald's sign
on the bottom. This is what our money is being spent on. There is no restraint on money to subsidize interest on loans of over $600 million to the Soviet Union to build gas pipeline facilities.
The restraint is on what the people of Canada want. Talk to them. Talk to them in your riding, Mr. Speaker, or the ridings of Lincoln, Parkdale or Hamilton West. Ask them whether they would rather have restraint on foreign aid programs or restraint on medicare.
The people of Canada are not concerned about which government pays the bill. There is only one taxpayer. The established programs financing act is part of the fiscal arrangements of all of Canada. It happens to be convenient in order to spread the risk in Canada. It happens to be convenient in order to make sure that we have decent medical and postsecondary education facilities across the country. That is the way we organize a co-operative federalism.
This government does not give a damn about co-operative federalism. Because these programs may, under the Constitution, fall within the ambit of provincial responsibility, the government is prepared to say they are open to drastic cuts, almost a billion dollars this year, $1 billion next year and $2 billion in two years. That is the attitude of this government clearly expressed by the hon. member for Mississauga North. That is where the restraint is going to be.
That hon. member will have restraint even in his part of Mississauga where a new hospital is to be built. He will have us restrain the growth of that hospital as well as the medical fees to doctors. There will be reduced services for his constituents and mine. We live in the same city. That is the restraint he would have.
He is quite prepared to vote for more foreign aid, a larger budget for the CBC and more Liberal advertising bunko on television. He is prepared to vote and to recommend, as his minister does, that medical services be cut back, that funds for Erindale College and the University of Toronto be cut back. He would have cutbacks for young people trying to build a future because the expenditures are not made directly by the federal government but are financed in co-operation with the provincial governments.
Some effort was made in the bunko leading up to this proposal by the Government of Canada that the provinces were not carrying their weight. The purpose of our amendment is to allow a task force to inquire into that in order to find out how these established programs should be financed. We say there should be another two years so this can be properly looked at.
I want to bring to the attention of hon. members evidence produced before tha task force committee with respect to medical services. The federal government's share of provincial health programs was 47.9 per cent in 1979-80. In 1980-81 it was 47.6 per cent. As the years go by, this becomes smaller. Indeed, the outlook prepared by the Department of National Health and Welfare indicates that even if the established programs financing stays the same, the federal share of health
April 1, 1982

financing will continue to decrease. Therefore, all this talk about the provinces not carrying their weight with respect to health care financing is nonsense. All the members opposite have to do is to read the documentation produced by the Department of National Health and Welfare to the task force and produced on April 14, 1981, in, of all things, a slide presentation.

speechtext:
It is a slime presentation today, but the truth is what they said in April, 1981. It is slime today because they do not say the same now as they said in April, 1981. Today, in the mirage and smoke and mirrors of tax points, they say they are not cutting. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), bless her soul, is totally incapable of calculating anything. As a matter of fact, she takes pride in the fact that she cannot make a calculation. She says in the House that she is increasing health expenditures by 13.4 per cent. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance says that we are ripping them off by $937 million this year. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says there will be a 13.4 per cent increase and he says there will be $937 million less.
Well, it does not take a great deal of intelligence to read the figures-maybe grade three learning. The hon. member for Mississauga North has at least that level of education and he can tell us the correct figures. In fact, he has told us the correct figures and perhaps he could go to the ministry of health and give its minister some correct figures.
While he is doing this, he might as well talk to the minister in charge of lotteries. I say the minister in charge of lotteries because the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) has abandoned any claim he has to represent the interests of post-secondary education. He is the minister of lotteries and the minister of "gimmes", the quick buck fix. He has no intention of giving fair consideration to what is happening. He indicates that education spending is rising by 12 per cent, but the member for Mississauga North is correct-the budgets are being cut and cut drastically. These cuts will apply to every student, teacher and everyone who wishes to progress and better himself in our society.
We hear stories of libraries being cut back and publications going down the drain. Witnesses who have appeared before the committee have told us that. Essential community courses such as English as a second language are being cut out because they are no longer essential. People are told it is no longer essential because they speak the language of the country. This is the kind of attitude which the government takes toward development which is necessary to make our country grow and prosper again.
Cuts are taking place in some of the most essential services. These cuts are occurring because of the intention of government to restrain its expenditures. There is no restraint by this government. Its intention is to eliminate moneys over which
Federal Transfers to Provinces
they do not have absolute control. It is an attempt to make the provinces pick up a deficit in some areas so that it can have a larger deficit in other areas. The government is not showing restraint; it is only attempting to transfer deficits.
The hon. member for Mississauga North said that maybe I am a spender. We are not talking about a change in spending patterns. We are discussing the question of established programs. This is a new spending program for new foreign aid ventures, new spending for new CBC development, new spending for new advertising ventures. This is ensuring that the medical health care systems we have are retained and that the established education programs which we have organized in Canada remain.
When our party proposed that the existing programs be extended for two years, it is because there has been a feeling across the country that the provinces have not paid their share over the years. Therefore, if that is the case, we make the same suggestion as the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada has made. Let us have a task force on education to find out who should finance these programs. Should they be financed by a voucher system, as suggested by the Secretary of State? Should they be financed as they presently are? Should they be financed by a 50-50 contribution between federal and provincial governments? Perhaps they should be financed by direct grants to universities and colleges from the federal government, but certainly we should have an inquiry into the subject, which is the reason for proposing a two-year hoist on the matter. Any sensible Liberal member would accept that suggestion.
The same argument applies to health causes. We have evidence of people having to wait from three to six months for a hospital room in order to get to the operating room. We have evidence of people who are in fact dying because they cannot be operated on for a heart condition. We have evidence of people who must lie on stretchers in hospital corridors and some who can only get into a hospital because of an emergency. These incidents must stop. I suggest that the government members, and particularly backbenchers in the government, must fulfil their obligation to their constituents and recognize what is happening to our established programs.

speechtext:
I will repeat here what I said in the committee. As far as the revenue guarantee is concerned, I was opposed to its continuance. I said that in committee previously,

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
said that in committee today and I am repeating it on the floor of the House tonight. I was not in favour of the continuance of the revenue guarantee which has already been continued for five years too long.
With respect to the effect of the discontinuance, since 1972 the provinces were supposed to readjust their financing by themselves within the ensuing five-year period as they have the right to levy their own taxes as they see fit. There is absolutely no logical reason at all for continuing this payment.
However, I would like to make an important point. It is that the revenue guarantee was approximately $800 million this year. If the hon. member for Mississauga South is honest he will know that in the spring of this past year, 1981, when we were reviewing the amount which was being transferred to the provinces in the past year-we had the estimates-we were looking at transfers in fiscal equalization amounting to approximately $3.4 billion, of which $1.7 billion was going to my own province of Quebec.
What the opposition has chosen to ignore is that a program of equalization is based on the capacity of various provinces. During this past year there has been a change in the amount that has been paid due to necessity. In fact, the province of Quebec during this year which has just terminated on March 31, 1982, will have received from the equalization program a total of $2.1 billion, or $400 million more. For the total program, including all Maritime provinces, the increase alone was over $800 million. I am not referring to the increase that applies to the Canada Assistance Plan. If you consider those amounts combined, the amount that the provinces received extra in the last year which they could not possibly have counted upon at April 1, at the beginning of last year, is in excess of $1 billion. Therefore, anyone who does not talk about that but chooses to talk only about what they see as cuts on the other side is giving a false impression.
He made another point with which I do not agree. He said they want to dispose of the revenue guarantee, which they cannot control. Will he please acknowledge that post-secondary education funding is completely and unconditionally transferred? There is nothing which obliges the provinces to use these moneys for post-secondary education and, in fact, there are two provinces to which the federal government transfers more in cash than those provinces actually spend. I want that on the record too.

speechtext:
Furthermore, when it comes to health care, we transfer a sum on a per capita basis or on a population basis. It is block funding but, in essence, right across the board we transfer an equivalent sum per province according to its population. Once again, although the funds are earmarked for a certain purpose, we do not decree the amount that should be spent on health care. That is a provincial decision, and if there is any reduction in services, the responsibility is one hundred per cent that of the provinces.
Today a very right wing group, the Canadian Medical Association, appeared before the committee and gave evidence which annoyed me intensely. I will quote some of its remarks as follows:
We see no reason why the Government of Canada must give every province exactly the same amount of money per capita for health care regardless of the health care needs or financial ability of the provinces. We see no reason why the Government of Canada should not promote reasonably comparable health services in every part of this country by providing 60 per cent or 70 per cent of health care costs in some provinces and only 40 per cent or 30 per cent in richer ones. Why not incorporate the principle of equalization into federal support of medicare? Why not establish a program earmarking federal health care funds directly related to the health care needs and inversely related to the fiscal capacity of the provinces?
I had to laugh when I heard that and after listening to the approach of that association today because it seemed to me that it would mean less money going to the richer provinces and more going to the poorer provinces, which is a means of equalization. I do not oppose that, but I merely say that if we take these figures and extrapolate them according to the populations of the richer and poorer provinces, the net effect will be a transfer of fewer dollars, and to me that does not make too much sense.
The point is that, in fact, the amount of money that has been transferred in the past year, which ended yesterday, has increased, by the very nature of the programs themselves, by more than $1 billion. That is $1 billion that the provincial governments could not have included in their budgets for this past fiscal year. And it is equally possible, depending on the way the economy goes in the ensuing year, that there could be equivalent increases.
Hon. members opposite continually harp on the fact than any reduction in services is a federal responsibility. First, the federal government does not control in any way the spending of funds for health care. Second, the federal government does not even earmark transfers for post-secondary education which, as I have indicated, in some cases amount to more than the amount spent by the provinces. The federal government transfers unconditionally all equalization payments to the provinces. When the federal government pays the bill for the Canada Assistance Plan, it writes the cheque according to the amount a province decides to spend. The decision in each one of those programs rests entirely with the provincial governments. As long as the federal government is transferring 20 per cent of its budget to provincial treasuries for responsibilities which are entirely provincial, I do not think the provinces should come back and spit in our face for our generosity.

The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada appeared before the task force and in part indicated:

Obviously, the federal government cannot continue its commitment to minimum standards of human services and at the same time reduce expenditures in the social affairs envelope.

Services currently funded by the Canada Assistance Plan and the Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons' Act, are widely admitted to be in their early developmental stages. The council is calling for more expenditures, not just because they would improve services. In fact, many of those expenditures would save money. Providing a part-time worker to go into the home of a senior citizen who cannot manage by himself may cost $25 per day under home care. It would cost $200 or $250 per day for the same person to be in hospital, as so many of them are. We should not be cutting back or reducing our services. -the impact of specific federal reductions will be generalized and spread over all social programs by provincial budgetary processes. I will not say that this Liberal government is being as brutal as President Reagan is in the United States, but it is a matter of degree, not a very big difference in degree. What we are seeing, however, are the first steps in the same kind of process, that has been such a disaster in the United States.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in view of the time this evening-and I know other members of the House want to speak-I will try to be as brief as possible.
The House might be somewhat surprised in terms of who the mover and the seconder of this amendment are, but I want to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for seconding the motion.
This matter arises from the situation that has developed through the negotiations in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements as they affect Manitoba particularly. I said during second reading debate, and others in this House have said it as well, that I did not want to be provincial or parochial in the debate, but when one looks at the figures in terms of the equalization formula, one finds that without question the formula impacts on Manitoba most severely. People who have studied the formula, quite apart from those who come from the province in which I reside, generally agree about the impact. You will find there is a non-partisan approach to this matter in terms of the Progressive Conservative Party, the New Demo-cractic Party here, and in fact, members of the Manitoba legislature, and it is on that basis that I raise it.
The debate that has taken place so far, and I do not want to reflect on the preceding voice vote, has generally focused on the established programs financing and cutbacks in that field. That matter has been dealt with very adequately in the amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). In terms of waiting for two years, they were not simply there to delay for the sake of delay but to be utilized for the purpose of negotiation, accommodation and agreement. That was the purpose. But what is unique is that the equalization formula is the major crux of the problem faced in Manitoba.
Prior to the negotiations that took place, we had the ten-province base. Then, when the federal government came in with its proposal, it brought in the Ontario base. The fear at that time was that Ontario as a province could become eligible for equalization payments. The argument then was that Ontario should not be eligible for equalization and, no matter what the financial factors were in Ontario relative to the rest of the country, Ontario would always be the base. That obviously reflected negatively on the province of Ontario, in fact, on the formula generally. Consequently, there was an amendment whereby a five-province base was used, the so-called have provinces.
The province I want to reflect on today is the province of Manitoba. Mr. Speaker, we heard in committee today the finance minister of Manitoba saying a number of startling things. He pointed out that his province would continue to face record high deficits for the next five years. We do not know what they will be, but the general projection is a minimum of $300 million per year. This will impact severely on that province's taxpayers not only in the sense of increased taxation but, equally importantly, on the ability to maintain national standards. That is another reason for the amendment by the
April 1, 1982
hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. The fact is that Manitobans would have to lower their standards of health care and post-secondary education, which is unacceptable. The question then remains whether adjustments could be made in the transitional period to lessen the impact on Manitoba.
The Manitoba finance minister also said that while their deficit would increase, the federal government's deficit would decrease. 1 do not agree with the second part of that equation. When I look at the federal government's deficit position, my fear is that it is going to increase for the following reasons. As the economy flattens out, the Minister of Finance's projections in his November 12 budget concerning the deficit are out the window. In addition, the National Energy Program has had the effect of lowering the output of the have provinces. The province of Alberta, on which a lot of revenue projections were based, has not seen the growth projected in the NEP and in the energy agreement between Alberta and Canada.
Mr. Speaker, could we have some order?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, I think the reduced deficit projections are now out the window. So what does the federal government do? Is there a transitional point whereby, for example, Manitoba would not be affected as greatly as it is under the five-province base? A number of us have looked at that question, and that is why you have the amendment. I said I would not be too long because I do not want to infringe on the time of other members, but the amendment proposes the following. I know there have been meetings with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and I think even he has been somewhat surprised at the negative impact the equalization formula has had on Manitoba. What is being proposed is that the percentage share of equalization for Manitoba could not be less than the second worst percentage of any given year, relative to the other have-not provinces. The figures show, Mr. Speaker, that in 1982-83, Manitoba would receive equalization payments of 10.7 per cent, when the national average will be 13.6 per cent. In 1983-84 it would receive 10.7, when the national average will be 11.3 per cent. In 1984-85 it would receive 10.7 per cent, when the national average will be 10.5 per cent. In 1985-86 it would receive 10.7 per cent, when the national average will be 10.3 per cent, and in 1986-87 it will be 10.1 per cent, when the national average will be 10.3 per cent.
You will find, Mr. Speaker, and I mention this because of the transitional period-which is why the hon. member's amendment appeals to me because it impacts very heavily on Manitoba in the first two years-that we would be willing, if that amendment were carried, to let this amendment go by because I think we would then have taken care of that first two-year period. So in order to meet that transition problem for Manitoba, we are proposing to use the second worst percentage formula, if I can describe it in that fashion. If
April 1, 1982

one looks at the formula today, Manitoba would lose $582 million net over five years. It was $747 million, but the Minister of Finance recognized the disparity and the loss has been reduced. So there has been recognition that a problem exists. I am simply saying that Manitoba taxpayers cannot afford to be locked into an equalization formula for five years which will impact on their ability to maintain national standards.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, there is the question of whether the amendment is in order. I know members who serve on the committee are familiar with the argument that, on the basis of the House rules and because it involves some $300 million over the life of the formula, the amendment is in violation of the royal prerogative in that the expenditure of public funds has to be a government initiative. Well, I accept that. If the government, for example, wants to move this amendment, or if it wants to modify it, I would be willing to look at the modification. I would be willing to have the government, after the discussions it has had, move an amendment similar to this one. The seconder of the motion can speak for himself, but I think he would want to consider that as well. We are simply saying that we do not approach this on a provincial, parochial or selfish basis. Rather, if we believe in equalization as it is to be entrenched in the Constitution, then surely it stands to reason that before we do that on April 16 we must have in place an equalization formula which is in fact not an equalization formula. We could have used any formula, for example the Alberta formula, and then everyone would have been eligible. I would suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher)-and he is in the House tonight-that if he is willing to examine this question from the suggested perspectives, 1 would be willing to discuss with him what modifications should be made. If he wants to adopt the amendment as his own, I accept that, but I say to him that the manner in which this equalization formula impacts on the taxpayer of Manitoba is not fair. Therefore, I commend the amendment to members of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the seconder of the motion now before the House I would like to add to what the hon. member for Prove'ncher (Mr. Epp) has said about the reason this particular amendment is so important. It is only days before the new Constitution is proclaimed here in Canada. Equalization payments to the provinces will be included as part of the very Constitution of Canada. If we are able to proclaim that particular section of the Constitution with any kind of integrity and consistency, then I think the amendment now before the House must be approved by the House. The amendment would redress the way in which the province of Manitoba is now affected by the proposed equalization formula.
Before I go into any more of the arguments, I would like to put on the record what I know other hon. members have stated, even at second reading. I would like to tell the House about the way in which Manitoba is treated so unequally by this formula. In the first year of this five-year agreement, the percentage increase for Manitoba will be 9.9 per cent. What will it be for the other have-not provinces? It will range from
Federal Transfers to Provinces
21 per cent to 10 per cent. In the second year of this five-year agreement, the percentage increase for Manitoba will be 6 per cent. What will it be for the other have-not provinces? It will range from 14.4 per cent to 10.7 per cent. The third year is when Manitoba will really get kicked in the teeth. Our percentage increase will be 2.8 per cent. What will it be for the other have-not provinces? It will be 11.3 per cent, 11.2 per cent, 11.8 per cent, 11.4 per cent and 10.7 per cent, compared to our 2.8 per cent increase. In the fourth year, what will be the percentage increase for Manitoba? It will be 3.8 per cent. Again, we are looking at figures of 11 per cent and 10 per cent for all the other have-not provinces. In the fifth year we will get an increase comparable to the other provinces, around 10 per cent.
The over-all effect is that over the five-year agreement Manitoba will receive a percentage increase in equalization payments of 37.2 per cent. The next lowest will be Quebec, at 66.1 per cent. That is from 37 per cent to 66.1 per cent. The other four have-not provinces, the Atlantic provinces, will all receive percentage increases in the 80 per cent range.
I simply ask, where is the justice? Where is the equalization in this? Where is the equality in this particular kind of proposal? What madness, vindictiveness, error or absence of mind led the government to develop and then to propose a formula which would treat a particular province, the province of Manitoba, in such a way? I am simply baffled. I am sincerely baffled as to why the government picked this particular formula out of all the formulas it could have picked. Other formulas would still have had the effect of reducing the government's over-all payments through equalization but would not have singled out any province as much as the province of Manitoba has been by this particular formula.
I therefore plead with hon. members on the government side to consider seriously the fact that this amendment has been moved with the support of both opposition parties. The government ought to consider making this amendment its own and bring it in before this bill goes forward.
What would be the effect of the amendment? The effect of the amendment would not be to bring Manitoba up to the highest level, to make sure that Manitoba gets exactly as much as everyone else. We realize that the formula, in order to stay a formula, must be treated with a certain amount of respect. Manitoba differs, in its fiscal capacity, from the Atlantic provinces. All this amendment asks is that in every year of that five-year agreement, Manitoba be paid a percentage increase which is at least as much as that paid the second worst province out of the six have-not provinces. That seems to me to be a rather humble proposal. We are not asking to be elevated to the top. All we are asking is that Manitoba be treated the same as the second worst province, as it works out in this formula.
I do not see any reason the government cannot accept this proposal. I want to put it very bluntly to the only two Liberal members from Manitoba. If this amendment is not passed and if the government does not make this amendment its own, I

I am quite serious, but I look across at the hon. members, and they are smiling, having a bit of a jape among themselves. If they think this will not have some political impact on their fortunes in Manitoba, then they are kidding themselves. God knows, it could not get much worse, but they still do elect people out there. This will have an effect on the province of Manitoba and that effect will be made known to the voters of Manitoba by the provincial government and by members of both the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party.
There is an argument which has been offered concerning the reason Manitoba should not be complaining too loudly about the way it is treated by this equalization formula. Just for those who might have the misfortune of hearing it, the argument is that payments to Manitoba in the last five-year period were quite generous and that the formula has just worked out differently this time. One gets lucky in one five-year period and the next five-year period one gets unlucky. We really got unlucky this time, but that is another matter.
The reason that the equalization payments to Manitoba appear to be so generous in the last five-year period is that they are viewed in relation to the payments it received in the five-year period before that. One cannot view these equalization payments as a little snap photograph in history somewhere and then say, "Look what you were getting last time." The equalization payments Manitoba received from 1977 to 1982 were higher because it had received a bad deal for 1972 to 1977. It seems that the Liberals go in cycles. Now it seems that we are supposed to get a bad deal again. However, as I tried to point out, this time we are really getting a bad deal. We are getting such a bad deal that one finds the province of Manitoba getting a percentage increase which is approximately half of what the second worst province in the formula receives, or 37.2 per cent as opposed to 66.1 per cent, which is what Quebec will receive over the next five years.
All we are asking in this amendment is that the province of Manitoba be raised up to the level of the second worst province
in the formula. 1 want to repeat Mr. Speaker, why would you have a formula that does this to one particular province? I cannot understand it. It does not make any sense.
When I came down here as a new Member of Parliament, it may be because I come from Manitoba-where we are a kind of combination of political and cultural values, with Ontario and the west and ourselves right smack in the middle-1 did not really have a kind of regional consciousness. I did not come down here to be a spokesman for Manitoba, I came down here to be a member of the Canadian Parliament and to figure out what to do for the whole country.
I must say that over the last few years, sitting here and looking over there, and seeing what can be done to rail service, seeing what can be done to the Crow or what is proposed to be done to the Crow, and the whole attitude of the government, I found myself developing more and more a regional consciousness here in the House. In a way I regret it. I did not come down here to see myself as a member from one region opposed to members from another region. The fact of the matter is that this is what is beginning to happen to me, and I regret it. After these last few weeks, after looking at a formula that treats my home province in this particular way, I cannot say that I am exactly on my way to retreating from that regional consciousness of which I spoke.
I plead with the hon. members, on the government side in particular, not to allow this present equalization formula to go through in the way it is. It would be a tragedy for Manitoba, it would also be a tragedy for our whole view of equalization. It makes a mockery of the very notion of equality between the provinces and the ability of all provinces, no matter which province it may be, to provide public services at reasonably comparable levels.
We had some other amendments to move, Mr. Speaker. I want to mention some. We moved them in committee. If we spend all our time now and we vote on this amendment, so be it, because this is one of the most important amendments in this particular package. I am going to sit down so that others can have a chance to speak.
I want to put on the record that in order to pay more attention to this particular proposal we have forgone our opportunity to debate our amendment dealing with the way in which the federal government is discriminating against the province of Saskatchewan by not forgiving them what the province of Saskatchewan owes them due to census readjustment, when we are forgiving all the other provinces that owe the federal government money.
We have forgone our amendment which tries to get rid of the GNP cap that the Liberals have put on the equalization payments. That is another way of deconstitutionalizing equalization payments, by saying that equalization has its limits and it is going to be tied to the GNP. We have forgone that amendment.
April 1, 1982

There is one other amendment that we have forgone that 1 want to mention. It is one in which we want to build into this fiscal package an opportunity for review before the next fiscal arrangements are negotiated, in the same way as happened in an ad hoc way, as a result of the setting up of the special parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. I thought that was a particularly good exercise. I began to have my doubts about it as 1 listened to members of the very task force that I was on and who signed the same paper that I signed. Yet I saw the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) get up here and I can hardly believe that these are the same people with whom I spent 265 hours in hearings, and that those are the same people who signed the parliamentary task force report. That report made a lot of recommendations, and good recommendations, that this government has completely ignored, including some of the central recommendations, like the revenue guarantee, leaving the money attributable to the compensation in the revenue guarantee. This particular package was taken out; that was a main recommendation, but they ignored it.
Not having lost faith in democracy, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that by the next time we have that kind of review, we might have a different government. Who knows, we might even have a New Democratic government. Wouldn't that be the day! Then we would have a government that would pay attention to those people who come to these hearings and who give their views. We might pay attention to them. So, Mr. Speaker, I hope that we will pass this amendment, redress this injustice to Manitoba and then truly have the kind of equalization formula that we ought to have.

speechtext:
I would like to take a few minutes of the time this evening, Mr. Speaker, to make the case that the mover and seconder of this motion, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) have made.
When listening to this discussion and the debate that has gone on so far, I wondered whether someone coming here, listening to the debate for the first time, would wonder whether he was a citizen from another planet or from another part of the world. Someone capable of being a little more objective than many of us are would wonder whether we were talking about two separate sets of taxpayers; one set of taxpayers paying tax to the provincial government and one set of taxpayers paying tax to the federal government. It seems to me that we have lost sight of the fact that the same people whom we are discussing, asking whose ox is going to be gored, happen to be the same taxpayers of the country, whether they pay those taxes to the provincial government or to the federal government and whether they get the services back from the provincial government or from the federal government. It seems to me that we should be concerned about the taxpayers as citizens of the country who are expecting some services back for the taxes that they pay. If we could keep that in mind, we might have a better attitude to what goes on in the House and
Federal Transfers to Provinces
set a better example to those who watch the debate and the proceedings in the House.
It is up to us to set the proper tone, to realize that we should both be aiming at serving the people who pay the taxes and those who are expecting the services back-and in this case we are talking about the equalization payment.
I have two or three other quick points, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am glad to see that the parliamentary secretary is here and paying close attention. I know he has a close relative in Manitoba. It is not that I expect anything in the way of a favourable decision or any judgment that he may have in this matter. I just point out that he has a relative who comes from Manitoba and, having regard to that, I expect he is well aware of the province and some of the problems we have there.
As to the point of whether we should or should not have more from the federal government I think that what concerns us in Manitoba-and this is a non-partisan topic in Manitoba, or at least it should be-is that whatever point has to be made for Manitoba, or whatever cuts there are, we expect they should be equal across the country.
All kinds of figures have been given by the two hon. members who spoke ahead of me. Many people talk about percentages and statistics. The point, to my mind, is that Manitoba, over the next five years, will receive an average increase of about one-third over what we have now, whereas the next lowest increase will be approximately two-thirds. Looking at it on that basis, it is not a small amount, it is a large amount. We will get about half as much, on average, as far as the increase goes over the next five years, as the lowest province next to us. So we are not talking about a few fractions or a few decimal points here and there, we are talking about almost half as much of an increase as the province of Quebec will get, which will be the next province above Manitoba.
When we are dealing with figures like this, it sometimes takes a long time to fully understand them, regardless of whether we want to be critical of the Department of Finance or the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or whoever is in power, and there is a possibility that something has been overlooked. I do not think we can use that excuse any more after tonight, because the issues have been well aired in committee and it has been well aired in the House of Commons. Up until now, if we wanted to be kind about it, we probably could have given the government the benefit of the doubt and said it was an honest mistake; but we are drawing the attention of the government to it this evening and hereafter I do not think that excuse will hold water any more, so clearly we have to make clear the position it is going to put Manitoba in by this new equalization formula.
It puts us in a particularly bad situation because, as the Manitoba minister of finance said this afternoon, talking about that province, "We are heading to greater deficits at the same time that the federal government is heading toward lower

April 1, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
deficits." There is another problem that we have. At the same time the federal government is attempting to lower its deficit, if Manitoba wants to maintain the services that have been provided in the past, there will be larger deficits for the province of Manitoba. I think all members will find that acceptable. One would expect the federal government to have some sympathy for that position if it believed its projections and, if those projections come about, because the federal government is heading toward a lower deficit.
Another point needs to be made with regard to the equalization formula. Over the past number of years our record in terms of economic growth has stayed relatively constant. As the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill said, there is no reason why over the next five years we should be treated so much worse than the average. It appears there is nothing, in terms of the formula, which would cause us to be treated less well in terms of less equalization payments than we have been in the past.
I really cannot understand why this amendment should not be passed. I do not want to get into the threats made by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill. We do not threaten to campaign against the two Liberal members who have been elected in Manitoba. We want to get the job done for the citizens of Manitoba. If the government would take that kind of attitude, it would see fit to support this amendment. Whether it be in the name of the mover and seconder is immaterial. We are interested in seeing that the citizens of Manitoba are treated equally, relative to other citizens throughout the country.
I wish to close by referring to something said in the throne speech on April 14, 1980, almost two years ago. In the throne speech it was said that Members of Parliament who are not government members have a special duty to represent those areas of the country that are not represented by government members. On the other hand, we have a special duty to represent our part of the country here in the house and to represent Canada in our constituencies. This is an opportunity for the government to put that into practice.
If we are to do a good job in terms of being federal members and standing up for our country, we have to be treated fairly. I throw that admonition back to the government members to ensure that we are not treated unfairly in Manitoba, so that we can be proud to be part of this part of the country and are treated fairly.
I do not want to prolong the debate. I hope that the two Manitoba members who sit on the government side will prevail upon the government to correct what is obviously a very bad situation for Manitoba when you look at the equalization payments in the new formula.
