speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure once again to comment on Bill C-97 following the three previous speakers, especially the last one who reminded me so touchingly of my close family ties in Manitoba. I am not sure whether it is appropriate or not but I would like to take
this occasion to say hello directly to those members of my family who might be watching right now. It is a real pleasure.
Before I go into some of the arguments on the other side, I would like to put on the record again, as was done earlier today, some of the statistics that are involved. This will help the people of Manitoba to cut through the rhetoric that has been thrown out by all parties.
This year $895 million will be going to the people of Manitoba under the equalization and established programs financing. Over the next five years that will grow until 198687, when $1,280 million will be sent out. That gives a grand total of $5,363 million. Included in those figures is a total of $165 million being sent to Manitoba to help that province in the change from one calculating formula to another. That $165 million is broken down as follows: $82 million this year, $56 million next year and $27 million in the third year. It is a diminishing transition payment intended to cushion the blow of moving from one formula to another.
There is a third payment that has not been included in these calculations, that is, $31 million going to Manitoba in the form of forgiveness for some calculations on population size. That $31 million was included in payments made previously. When the new population figures were provided, it was found we had overpaid by that amount. That amount technically is being forgiven. That is an extra $31 million for the province of Manitoba.
This afternoon in committee and now in the House we have heard talk about the formulas and the basis for calculating them as if there were some kind of competition between the provinces. That is misleading. Equalization payments are exactly that; equalization payments make provinces equal to a mathematical standard. The minister clearly explained this when he visited the committee last Monday. 1 would like to pass along a couple of comments which the minister made. He said:
The formula Is intended to bring all provinces up to a standard ... Obviously, at a certain stage, particular provinces get close to that standard, and because of that the yield of equalization decreases and some provinces slip out of the equalization formula because of their improved fiscal capacity.
The minister pointed out a couple of other things, particularly with respect to Manitoba. He said it is still true that even with the transitional payment, calculating the rate of growth percentage-wise year to year in certain years, the rates of growth for Manitoba are less than for the Atlantic provinces or Quebec. He answered by saying:
If an equalization system is to measure fiscal capacity it cannot yield similar results for every province.
In other words, let we remind our friends from the NDP of one of the age-old principles that they like to present to the Canadian people; that is: from each according to his ability; to each according to his need.
We do not give the same amounts to every province. For example, we do not yet give any equalization to Ontario. Bill Davis might put us in the position where we eventually have to make an equalization payment to Ontario, but we are not yet in that position. Should Ontario then come to us and say that
April 1, 1982

it is receiving less equalization on a percentage basis than Manitoba and therefore it should get a special grant to make up for that? It sounds ridiculous. It is equally ridiculous for Manitoba to say that it is receiving less than the Atlantic provinces and therefore it should get some flat payment in forgiveness. That is what is being presented here, a kind of competition among the provinces where they would say: "Because we do not get as much on a percentage basis, we want a special payment." That is what the members are telling the federal government. I am sorry but I cannot agree with that.
Let us review some of the statistics involved. From 1976-77 to 1981-82, Manitoba's equalization entitlement had increased more rapidly than those of any other province. It went up in Manitoba by 156 per cent, and it went up in Nova Scotia by 72 per cent. How did this happen? Why did Manitoba get 156 per cent and Nova Scotia only 72 per cent?
The treasurer of Manitoba answered that question in the committee this morning. He said:
Over the last five years, the Manitoba economy has performed well below the national average, and a number of indicators, such as real growth, job creation and investment show our performance to have been the worst of any province.
Since the performance was bad, equalization payments were greater in order to lift Manitoba's share up to the national standards. Now that Manitoba is closer to that standard, the percentages will not be so high. It is a very simple calculation.

One might wonder why I would raise in the Canadian House of Commons what the Secretary of State for External Affairs described on Monday as a purely internal British matter. Therefore, although there should not be discussions in NATO itself, the joint membership of both countries in NATO should be a disposing factor toward a settlement.

I understand that both the U.S. and Dutch governments have expressed their concern to Great Britain that the capability of Gibraltar's naval facilities could be gravely compromised unless time is given for the people of Gibraltar to make the transition from a defence-based economy to a tourist-based economy. At the very least, Mr. Speaker, Canada and our NATO allies should prevail upon the British government to phase out at least its financial commitment to the Gibraltar dockyard over a five or ten-year period so that the transition just described could be achieved. We are talking about a very small place in a sea of English language culture and a sea of other cultures in the Mediterranean.
I think it is incumbent upon members of this House to speak in defence of the people of Gibraltar who have valiantly fought to preserve their culture and linguistic traditions of the past 300 years. It is for this reason, and for the strategic reasons of NATO and Canada's role in NATO, that I bring this matter to the attention of the House this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FUTURE OF GIBRALTAR WITHIN NATO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) for bringing this very important matter not only to the attention of the House publicly but, also, to the attention of members of the House of Commons and the Government of Canada.
The question is, are we affected as an ally with the closure of the royal naval dockyard in Gibraltar. We are concerned, but we have to caution our concern in these terms. Canada has no mandate to speak for the people of Gibraltar. Gibraltar is a British dependent territory. Therefore, it is essentially a question for Britain's domestic policy.
The history of Britain in Gibraltar goes back 278 years to 1704 during the war of the Spanish succession when Sir George Rooke took possession of Gibraltar. The possession was ratified legally in 1713 by the Treaty of Utrecht. We are not talking about something that is recent, but something that is directly within British jurisdiction for 278 years.
We are encouraged in Canada by the fact that the British government has a white paper entitled "The United Kingdom Defence Program: The Way Forward". In it, the government of the U.K. unequivocally acknowledges its obligation to support the economy of Gibraltar. Let us face it, Mr. Speaker, without the dockyard the economy of Gibraltar would be crippled. Under this paper the U.K. government confirms it is prepared to consider alternate means of investment if there is a dockyard closure. We have every faith that the U.K. government will honour its white paper-because it has historically looked to Gibraltar, and consequently we feel the issue of Gibraltar should not be raised at NATO at this time, whether inside that organization or through bilateral discussions with NATO members.
Having said that, I again want to thank the hon. member for raising this issue in the House. Historically we feel a part of Gibraltar, and it is appropriate that members of this House remind us of that from time to time.

HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-REQUEST THAT LOANS BE GRANTED TO AFFECTED HOME OWNERS. (B) REFINANCING OF HOMES. (C) USE OF FUNDS ALLOCATED FOR HOME RENOVATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 24, 1982, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if the Government of Canada, through CMHC, would give consideration to amending the National Housing Act to permit CMHC to make direct loans to people having trouble renewing mortgages or refinancing their homes due to the presence of urea formaldehyde foam insulation, which, from now on, I will call UFFI.
The subject was first brought up when we were discussing the housing bill in committee with the minister responsible for CMHC. At that time I asked the president of CMHC, if in fact under certain circumstances CMHC made direct loans to home owners. He confirmed that under certain circumstances they do, such as in resource communities where it is difficult to obtain private financing. I suggested to the minister that he consider bringing an amendment to the act to allow CMHC to do this. It would not cost the taxpayer any money, the loans would be at current rates, and it would help people who have a very serious problem.
Unlike the government, I feel it must assume some responsibility with respect to the UFFI problem. After all, a government corporation provided the UFFI to the people who put it in their homes. It gave grants through the CHIP program to those who used it in their homes, so it has to accept some responsibility, and this is one area where I feel it can.
April 1, 1982

I brought up the case of Mr. Jim Rogers of Norval, who happened to work in the insulation business. To set an example, I guess he insulated his own home with UFFI and then did a number of others. I gather from those who have had the insulation installed that he did an excellent job. When the government banned the insulation, he of course lost his franchise, his business, the special equipment he purchased, his truck and so on, and he went bankrupt. During his financial difficulties he lost his family and is now on the verge of losing his home because the people who provided private financing for his home have now purchased their own homes and want their money. At the end of May he will not have a mortgage on his home. He has gone to various lenders and they will not provide financing. He has a unique problem, one that I think the government has a responsibility to do something about. The solution is simple: CMHC can provide direct loans to people who are having trouble financing.
Another example is Mr. Gerald Prevost of Georgetown. He has a second mortgage on his property and, because of this insulation problem, he cannot refinance that privately held second mortgage. It is being called and he is, therefore, also going to have trouble keeping his property.
1 plead with the government to take another look at the matter. The minister responsible for housing brushed it off in committee, said it was not his responsibility. The Prime Minister said they were already doing enough for the people suffering from this particular problem, which is not true.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is remaining quiet about the whole thing. I plead with him to take another look at it.
In the one minute left remaining to me, I would also like to say that 1 suggested in the same series of questions that if the $30 million designated to create employment and to add to RRAP-the home improvement program-could be ear-' marked to remove the urea formaldehyde foam insulation, or help with a portion of the costs of removing it from homes which would not otherwise qualify under the program which the government has already set up, this would create more jobs than the government has proposed, because it would be so labour-intensive. At the same time, it would help to clear up the very serious problem in this country caused by the use of urea formaldehyde foam insulation.
With those two thoughts, I leave it with the government. I ask it to give serious consideration to those two programs. It will not cost the taxpayer a penny more than permitted now, and it will help with a very serious problem.

I think all hon. members on each side of the House would like to be fully aware of just how much the government is doing to assist the owners of homes with formaldehyde insulation.
One of the first steps taken by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was to establish the information and coordination centre on urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The centre has served as a focus for the government program by providing advice and information to thousands of concerned home owners. The centre has carried out an extensive testing program involving houses from coast to coast.
A new program was announced in December to help people who are experiencing serious problems and to restore confidence in the value of UFFI homes. The government, as the minister mentioned in question period today, is providing free tests on demand to determine whether the formaldehyde is above the acceptable level. This started on March 22, and several thousand more test kits are going out this week. It also provides for technical advice and assistance to home owners, registration of qualified contractors and laboratories and financial assistance to a maximum of $5,000.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue in more detail a question 1 directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on March 24 dealing with the expansion of the Charlottetown airport. My question dealt with the delay of the necessary approval of Treasury Board to proceed with construction of the airport.
In order to understand the anxiety we Islanders are feeling, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to know that this matter goes back to 1974 at which time a federal-provincial planning committee agreed that a new air terminal building and a new cross-winds runway would be constructed on the present location of the Charlottetown airport. Following this, agreements were reached with the federal, the provincial and the municipal governments on a number of items, these being an environmental plan, public participation, zoning regulations, water and sewer hookup, diversion road construction, airport access interchange, and the airport terminal building.
The original terminal design was done in 1977; it featured a unique open design, a large tourist promotion area, rampside visibility, a children's play area, extensive landscaping, a VIP lounge and energy conservation features. The cost, in 1977 dollars, was $5,861,500.
On November 3, 1977, Treasury Board announced that tenders would be called for construction of the first phase, early in 1978, and it approved $21,531,500, subject to the following conditions: (a) The terminal building design be reviewed with a view to reducing its size and cost because of revised passenger forecasts; (b) annual reports be submitted to update the total cost, taking inflation into account; and (c) there be no increases in project scope. This resulted in a complete review of the passenger forecast figures which had been done in 1973-74 and upon which the size of the airport terminal was established.
In the early summer of 1978, three alternatives were put before the then minister of transport, the Hon. Otto Lang. They were: (a) proceed to Treasury Board with the original concept; (b) reduce the cost of the original concept; or (c)- and this is the one the minister chose-amend the original project by using a "Step" air terminal building modular design with a separate control tower.
During the summer of 1981, Mr. Speaker, discussions took place between officials of Transport Canada and the province of Prince Edward Island. The provincial officials were successful in pointing out the problems with congestion and the safety hazards connected with parking at the present terminal building. Transport Canada, with the assistance of the department of highways and public works, increased the present terminal building and included a new baggage-handling system. Transport Canada has assured the province that these minimal improvements are only temporary and it is hoped that the new air terminal building will be started in the summer of 1982.
The minister and I have had a fair amount of communication regarding this matter over the past few years, Mr. Speaker, and I am confident that he would like to see this issue settled almost as much as I would.
On February 11, I questioned the minister further on the delay and he promised to send me a letter giving me the agenda for coming developments. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the minister's exact words were: "The Charlottetown airport is on my mind all the time, with the Crow, at the moment; but I have not really been able to memorize the work agenda for each of Canada's one thousands airports, so I beg permission to send my friend a detailed analysis of every step in the coming hours."
Following question period, the minister and I did have a chance to talk but he did not give me a date as to when this matter is going to Treasury Board, although he did provide me with other related information.
On March 24, I asked the minister when the submission was going to Treasury Board. He replied that when I asked him the same question the other day he gave me a full report with a timetable and agenda and so on. He also indicated that if the submission did not go to Treasury Board exactly on the hour that he indicated, he would find out and report back as precisely as he did the last time. You have to give the minister points for being consistent. He has consistently told me he would provide me with an answer and he has consistently failed to do so.
While we are optmistic that now that the ball has started to roll it will continue to do so, but we are also painfully aware that, unless that ball picks up a lot of speed, the construction industry in P.E.I. will be facing an extremely bleak future. We appreciate the minister's support, but again we know that this redevelopment project also had the approval of the Hon. Otto Lang.
Mr. Speaker, those of us who make our home in Prince Edward Island, and who have been watching the so-called progress of the Charlottetown airport development over the years, know one thing for sure. We know that on November 3, 1977, Transport Canada received approval from Treasury Board for the redevelopment of the Charlottetown airport at a cost of $21,531,500. The present estimated cost of the project, including control tower and operations building, has now risen to $30,963,750. This is a disgraceful situation and should be rectified without further delay. Treasury Board must approve this project immediately so that we can get on with the job and provide a much needed facility, and also some relief to the construction industry of Prince Edward Island.

Redevelopment of the Charlottetown airport has evolved from a master planning study and has been conducted in cooperation with a joint federal-provincial planning committee, as indicated by the hon. member. It is expected that the final cost of the entire project will be in the $30 million range. Thus far, a combined services building has been erected at a cost of $2.2 million, and an aircraft parking apron and connecting taxi ways have been completed at a cost of $1.7 million. The hon. member will be pleased to know that the land acquisition program is proceeding well. Total cost of the program to date is close to $2 million.
